Article Title: No jobs, no visas! WFI prez blasts US embassy after wrestlers rejected: 'India lost out on gold medals'
Article Text:
WFI president Sanjay Singh

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Men's freestyle team cleared, others affected

Vishvajit More reaches historic final

India’s chances of winning medals at the U23 World Wrestling Championships 2026 in Las Vegas have been affected after nine Indian wrestlers were denied US visas.Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) president Sanjay Singh blamed the US Embassy, saying the wrestlers were rejected because they were under 20 and did not have full-time jobs.Speaking to IANS on Wednesday, Singh said the decision had cost India potential gold medals, with at least two of the wrestlers considered strong contenders. He also pointed out that the issue had never occurred in the tournament’s history."The US Embassy rejected the visas of nine Indian wrestlers on the grounds that they are unemployed. For the first time in history this has happened. Even the UWW president wrote to them regarding the matter," Singh said."This visa refusal is entirely the US Embassy's fault, and as a result, India lost out on gold medals. Among the nine wrestlers denied visas, at least two were strong gold medal prospects. India suffered a major medal loss due to the US Embassy's fault."All 10 members of India’s men’s freestyle team received permission to travel to Las Vegas. However, the visa issue affected the country’s Greco-Roman and women’s wrestling teams, leaving nine wrestlers unable to compete.The championships began with Greco-Roman events from October 12 to 14, followed by women’s wrestling from October 14 to 16. The men’s freestyle competitions are scheduled for October 16 to 18.Despite the setbacks, India has a chance to win gold through Vishvajit More, who reached the 55kg Greco-Roman final. He became the first Indian to reach a Greco-Roman final at the U23 World Championships in Las Vegas.More defeated Mexico’s Isaac Marin Mata 10-8, then beat U20 world champion Armin Shamsipour 8-1 before overcoming Russia’s Malik Gigiev 7-4 in the semifinals. The two-time U23 world bronze medallist will now face Georgia’s Koba Karumidze, aiming to become India’s first Greco-Roman gold medallist at the U23 Worlds.
Article Summary: Nine Indian wrestlers denied US visas for U23 World Wrestling Championships in Las Vegas. Wrestling Federation of India president Sanjay Singh blames US Embassy. At least two of the wrestlers were considered strong contenders for gold medals. Vishvajit More became the first Indian to reach a Greco-Roman final at the championships.

Article Title: ‘Ishan Kishan closing the gap’: Former India cricketer warns Rishabh Pant to raise his game
Article Text:
KL Rahul, Ishan Kishan, and Rishabh Pant

Ishan Kishan emerges as strong competition

Jaffer backs Pant’s match-winning ability

Former India opener Wasim Jaffer has warned Rishabh Pant that he needs to improve his performances to stay ahead of the competition for a place in the Indian Test team.Jaffer believes Ishan Kishan has improved significantly and is now closing the gap on Pant, while Dhruv Jurel is also competing for a spot.Pant has continued to play as India’s wicketkeeper in Test cricket, with Jurel featuring as a specialist batter in recent matches.However, Pant’s place in the national setup has come under discussion after he was dropped from the ODI and T20I teams and lost his vice-captaincy earlier this year.Jaffer said Kishan’s consistent performances across formats have made him a serious contender. He added that Pant needs to make the most of the upcoming domestic and IPL seasons to strengthen his position.“I would say Ishan Kishan, who has taken his game to a much higher level. At one point, it felt like Rishabh Pant was well ahead of Ishan Kishan. But now, it seems Ishan is steadily closing that gap. So, I feel this season will be very important for Rishabh Pant, whether it is the Ranji Trophy, the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy or the IPL. I think he will have to elevate his game. The gap is gradually narrowing, especially with Dhruv Jurel also in the mix.“Ishan Kishan has become so consistent across formats that, honestly, you don't see many wicketkeeper-batters ahead of him at the moment. KL Rahul is keeping wickets in ODIs, but Ishan is someone you can also play purely as a batter," Jaffer said in a video on his YouTube channel.Despite highlighting the growing competition, Jaffer praised Pant’s impact in international cricket. He compared the wicketkeeper-batter’s ability to deliver crucial innings to that of former Australia star Adam Gilchrist and said Pant could have scored many more centuries."You cannot put Rishabh Pant behind the others. He has played series-defining and match-winning innings on several occasions. He has been dismissed in the 90s so many times that I feel he might have scored another 10-15 centuries by now otherwise.“I think Rishabh Pant has been outstanding in such a short career. The kind of innings he has played is something I have rarely seen from anyone. We have obviously seen Adam Gilchrist do it, but after him, I don't think many players have produced such outstanding innings in such a short period," Jaffer added.Jaffer’s message was clear: Pant has an impressive record, but he must raise his game as competition for India’s wicketkeeper-batter position increases.
Article Summary: Pant has continued to play as India’s wicketkeeper in Test cricket. Jaffer believes Ishan Kishan has improved significantly and is now closing the gap on Pant, while Dhruv Jurel is also competing for a spot.

Article Title: Indian teenager partners with Pakistan’s Muhammad Yahya to win tennis title, reviving Indo-Pak Express memories
Article Text:
India’s Amrit Vats and Pakistan's Muhammad Yahya

A win that recalls the Indo-Pak Express

Can sport bridge the India-Pakistan divide?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Indian tennis player Amrit Vats and Pakistan’s Muhammad Yahya have teamed up to win the boys’ doubles title at the ITF World Tennis Tour Juniors J30 tournament in Djibouti.The pair defeated Thailand’s David Awayo and Saudi Arabia’s Ahmed Bahaa Srouji 6-2, 6-4 in straight sets.Their victory brings back memories of the famous Indian-Pakistani doubles partnership between Rohan Bopanna and Aisam-ul-Haq Qureshi, who earned the nickname “Indo-Pak Express” for their success on the international tennis circuit.Bopanna and Qureshi became one of tennis’ most recognised doubles teams, reaching the 2010 US Open men’s doubles final before losing to the Bryan brothers.The pair won five ATP titles together, including the 2011 Paris Masters, along with tournaments in Dubai, Johannesburg, Halle and Stockholm. Both also reached the top 10 in the doubles rankings.Beyond tennis, they used their partnership to promote peace between India and Pakistan through their ‘Stop War, Start Tennis’ campaign. They wore specially designed T-shirts to spread their message and received the Arthur Ashe Humanitarian of the Year award in 2010 for their efforts.Amrit and Yahya’s latest achievement recalls that period when athletes from the two neighbouring countries could compete together despite political tensions.India and Pakistan have long shared a complicated relationship, but sports have often provided opportunities for people from both countries to come together.In recent years, however, political tensions have increasingly affected sporting ties.Following the Pahalgam attack, India adopted a tougher stance towards Pakistan, with even customary handshakes between players becoming a point of discussion in cricket.Pakistan, meanwhile, have also resisted playing matches in India across various sports.The doubles victory in Djibouti does not change the wider political situation, but it offers a reminder that sporting partnerships can still bring Indian and Pakistani athletes together.Whether more such partnerships emerge will depend not only on the players but also on how relations between the two countries develop in the future.
Article Summary: Indian tennis player Amrit Vats and Pakistan’s Muhammad Yahya have teamed up to win the boys’ doubles title at the ITF World Tennis Tour Juniors J30 tournament in Djibouti. Their victory brings back memories of the famous Indian-Pakistani doubles partnership between Rohan Bopanna and Aisam-ul-Haq Qureshi.

Article Title: Kolkata to bring El Clasico to India with blockbuster Barcelona vs Real Madrid Legends clash on Nov 25: Luis Figo, Puyol among expected names
Article Text:
West Bengal sports minister Indranil Khan announced the November 25 El Clasico Legends blockbuster at Kolkata’s Salt Lake Stadium on Tuesday/ Image:X

Kolkata to host Barcelona vs Real Madrid Legends

Barcelona return to Kolkata after eight years

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Kolkata is preparing for another taste of El Clasico, with Barcelona and Real Madrid legends set to bring their famous rivalry to India on November 25. The exhibition will give fans another chance to see former stars of the Spanish giants together on Indian soil, following Real Madrid Legends’ victory in Mumbai last year. With Luis Figo, Carles Puyol and Iker Casillas among the names reportedly expected, the contest could be a significant occasion for a city with a long relationship with world football.West Bengal sports minister Indranil Khan announced on Tuesday that Barcelona Legends and Real Madrid Legends will meet at the Vivekananda Yuba Bharati Krirangan, popularly known as the Salt Lake Stadium, on November 25.The official squads have not yet been confirmed, although Portuguese great Figo, who represented both Spanish rivals during his playing career, and former Barcelona captain Puyol are among the prominent names expected to feature, alongside Spain’s World Cup-winning goalkeeper Casillas.This will be the second time the two clubs’ legends have faced each other in India, following their meeting at Mumbai’s DY Patil Stadium last year. Real Madrid Legends won that contest 2-0, with former striker Fernando Morientes and David Barral scoring the goals.The two sides also met in Miami earlier in 2026, playing out a 1-1 draw in which Martin Montoya scored for Barcelona and Álvaro Negredo found the net for Real Madrid.Their Kolkata encounter will now bring the exhibition rivalry to another Indian city, with the final line-ups still to be confirmed.For supporters, the appeal lies in seeing familiar names from two of football’s most celebrated clubs share the same pitch again. Figo’s unusual connection to both sides adds another layer of interest, while the prospect of Puyol and Casillas appearing gives fans further reason to watch for the official team announcements.Barcelona’s visit will mark their first appearance in Kolkata since September 2018, when they faced Indian football giants Mohun Bagan at the same stadium. The Catalans won that match 6-0, with Javier Saviola, Roger Garcia, Pedro Landi, Jari Litmanen and Jofre Mateu among the scorers.Kolkata has hosted some of football’s biggest names over several decades, earning a reputation as one of India’s most devoted footballing cities. One of its most memorable occasions came in 1977, when Brazilian legend Pelé led New York Cosmos against Mohun Bagan at Eden Gardens, while German giants Bayern Munich visited the city in 2008 to play the Kolkata club in a friendly.The city also hosted Lionel Messi’s only appearance on Indian soil in 2011, when Argentina faced Venezuela at the Salt Lake Stadium. More recently, the venue staged high-profile international friendlies in early October 2026, as India faced five-time world champions Brazil and two-time World Cup winners Uruguay.The November exhibition will add another prominent fixture to that history, bringing together two clubs whose rivalry has captivated football supporters across generations. Although the squads remain unconfirmed, Kolkata’s latest football occasion already has a clear attraction: another chapter of El Clasico, this time featuring the legends who helped make it famous.
Article Summary: Barcelona Legends and Real Madrid Legends will meet at Kolkata's Salt Lake Stadium on November 25. Luis Figo, Carles Puyol and Iker Casillas are among the prominent names expected to feature. It will be the second time the two clubs’ legends have faced each other in India, following their meeting at Mumbai’s DY Patil Stadium last year. The official squads have not yet been confirmed.

Article Title: Asian Para Games: Coach row, court battles, clearance delays deepen chaos
Article Text:
File Pic: Shooter Manish Narwal

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: With less than a week to go before the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Para Games starts, India’s preparations have been clouded by selection disputes, coaching omissions and administrative delays, leaving athletes in para shooting, cycling, badminton, table tennis and boccia grappling with uncertainty.On Monday, nine of India’s 13 selected para shooters met Sports Authority of India (SAI) officials and the sport’s project officer at SAI headquarters here, expressing dissatisfaction over the omission of chief coach J P Nautiyal from the contingent. Armourer and assistant coach Shivam Tyagi has also been left out.The aggrieved shooters urged authorities to reconsider the decision, with some expressing apprehension about competing without Nautiyal. Among those raising concerns were Manish Narwal, Mona Agarwal, Nihal Singh, Shrishti Arora, Swaroop Mahavir Unhalkar, Rakesh Nidagundi, Sumedha Pathak and Bhakti Sharma, who have won major international medals under his guidance.Bhakti, a deaf and non-speaking shooter who relies on specialised communication, reportedly broke down during the meeting, while Sumedha expressed doubts about competing without her coach.Pistol coach Rakesh Singh and support staff member Pavittar accompanied the shooters.The dispute comes as the ministry finally cleared the pending disciplines late on Monday evening, according to sources. The ministry’s push came as para badminton and table tennis contingents were scheduled to leave for Japan on Tuesday evening and there was considerable delay in announcing their final sanctions. With these approvals, the Indian contingent has been cleared across disciplines, barring pending court cases, including that of para cycling.The Oct 10 partial sanction covered eight disciplines and listed 128 athletes — 90 male and 38 female — alongside 91 officials, taking the contingent to 219 members. Badminton, table tennis and boccia were excluded at that stage.The delay also affected kit distribution. Athletes visiting the Paralympic Committee of India (PCI) office on Monday afternoon to collect ceremonial and competition kits returned empty-handed as approvals were awaited. Pramod Bhagat, India’s opening-ceremony flag-bearer, had worn fellow shuttler Sukant Kadam’s ceremonial outfit at the October 8 send-off because his own did not fit.Last-minute clearances have left athletes with little time to correct ill-fitting kits, organise equipment, and prepare for departure. In table tennis, competition begins on Oct 16, following classification checks on Oct 15. Wheelchair players need time to acclimatise and adjust their equipment, while paddlers will have just a day to rest after reaching Nagoya before classification begins.Despite the final approvals, five badminton names — Chirag Baretha, Manisha Patel, Shashank Kumar, Ammu Beulah Mohan and Rachna Patel — have not been sanctioned, sources said. LY Suhas has been cleared. Kalpesh Thakkar, secretary of the Table Tennis Association of Baroda, has also not been cleared.In para cycling, five qualified athletes have challenged their exclusion in the Delhi High Court under Articles 14 and 21, questioning the decision to retain only one cyclist despite six recommendations. The case will be heard again on Tuesday, with an interim decision expected.
Article Summary: Nine of India’s 13 selected para shooters met Sports Authority of India (SAI) officials. They expressed dissatisfaction over the omission of chief coach J P Nautiyal. The aggrieved shooters urged authorities to reconsider the decision. The dispute comes as the ministry finally cleared the pending disciplines late on Monday.

Article Title: Jithin’s stoppage-time strike helps NEUFC sink Mohun Bagan
Article Text:
Jithin MS after scoring in Guwahati on Monday. (Pic credit: NEUFC)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

They could not overcome the heavyweights in pre-season, losing in the semifinals of the Durand Cup and settling for a draw in the IFA Shield group stage.However, Juan Pedro Benali's men delivered when it mattered most as NorthEast United FC snatched a dramatic late 1-0 win against Mohun Bagan Super Giant in their Indian Super League opener in Guwahati on Monday.Playing in front of their fans at the Indira Gandhi Athletic Stadium, it was super-sub Jithin MS who struck the winner in the first minute of stoppage time after Bagan had dominated much of the 90 minutes with their attacks, while NEUFC relied on the brilliance of Alaaeddine Ajaraie to breach the visitors' defence.The first half produced some enthralling end-to-end action, with Mohun Bagan pressing from the word go and the Highlanders responding with attacks of their own after the opening 10 minutes.It was Lallianzuala Chhangte, in his new green-and-maroon colours, who dominated the early exchanges, having been named in the starting XI by coach Panagiotis Dilmperis ahead of regular Bagan winger Manvir Singh. Soon after, however, fellow new signing Lee Erwin began to grow into the game.The Scot also came closest to breaking the deadlock with a volley that dropped into the goal after hitting the bar, only for the offside flag to deny him.His physicality and pace began to pose all sorts of problems for the NEUFC defence. However, the Highlanders' new signing Nikhil Barla remained up to the task in his defensive role.The combination of Chhangte and Erwin made a Bagan breakthrough look imminent, only for the NEUFC defence, led by skipper Asheer Akhtar, to soak up the pressure every time.At the other end, Highlanders talisman Ajaraie looked threatening with his individual brilliance, while Ethyan Gonzalez's crosses repeatedly found runners inside the box, but each move was thwarted by the blocking and marking of Alberto Rodriguez and Lalengmawia Ralte.It was Rodriguez who came close for the visitors in the 43rd minute when his long-range effort whistled past the top-left corner of the NEUFC goal.While both coaches made a couple of changes after the break, it was the combination of Sahal Abdul Samad and Erwin that created two chances in quick succession in the 54th minute. Erwin first produced a feeble effort from close range after a Sahal pass and then failed to keep down a tricky volley, sending it over the bar.Soon after, Dilmperis replaced Erwin with Miguel Ferreira and brought on regular attackers Liston Colaco and Manvir Singh, along with Kashmiri forward Suhail Ahmed Bhat, in search of the elusive goal.Ajaraie had a couple of good chances in the 72nd and 75th minutes respectively but had Mehtab Singh stand strong with a tackle in the first while his dipping long volley that beat goalkeeper was disallowed by the referee’s whistle.On the other end, an incessant series of attacks from Bagan was met with some frantic but successful defending from the home side as Benali’s men mostly resorted to counter-attacks to find a goal against the run of play.Bhat could have got Bagan a goal towards the end when he failed to connect to a perfect cross from Colaco from the right at goal-mouth in the 87th minute and hit the woodwork a couple of minutes later.However, roared on by their fans, NEUFC began creating chances of their own towards the end of regulation time and, in the 95th minute, the ball fell to Jithin after a Gonzalez piledriver struck the woodwork. The dependable midfielder made no mistake, calmly turning the rebound into the winner.
Article Summary: NorthEast United FC snatch a dramatic late 1-0 win against Mohun Bagan Super Giant in their Indian Super League opener in Guwahati on Monday. Super-sub Jithin MS struck the winner in the first minute of stoppage time after Bagan had dominated much of the 90 minutes.

Article Title: From introduction to skeet gun at 13 to Asian Games bronze: Parinaaz Dhaliwal’s journey of precision, perseverance and the right support
Article Text:
Parinaaz Dhaliwal

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: For Parinaaz Dhaliwal, success in skeet shooting is about much more than hitting targets. It is a combination of technical precision, mental strength, financial backing and the ability to find balance under pressure. After years of investing in her game, the Asian Games medallist believes experience, the right coaching environment and an unwavering support system have helped her take significant strides forward.When Parinaaz looks back at her journey in shooting, she does not attribute her progress to one competition, one coach or one breakthrough moment. Instead, she sees it as an evolution shaped by years of training, international exposure and lessons learnt along the way. The bronze medal in the women’s skeet team event at the Asian Games 2026 at Aichi-Nagoya in Japan alongside Raiza Dhillon and Maheshwari Chauhan, was a significant milestone in that journey.“It was bits of everything, to be honest,” she says, reflecting on the difference between her previous Asian Games appearance and the latest campaign. “You evolve with every single competition. You learn something or the other.You win or you don’t win, but you always learn.”The medal was the culmination of a more comprehensive preparation programme, one that she believes made a tangible difference. Ahead of the Games, the Sports Authority of India (SAI), in coordination with the National Rifle Association of India (NRAI), organised two preparatory camps. The first, held in Aug, focused on fundamentals, while the Sept camp concentrated on fine-tuning and final preparations.The support structure, she says, was also stronger than before, with foreign coaching expertise and a larger team of support staff contributing to the preparations.An important part of that preparation was the presence of her personal coach, Anthony, an Olympic medallist from France. She received permission from the federation to have him join the national camp and accompany her to Japan, where he worked alongside national coaches and foreign coach Riccardo Filippelli.For her, the arrangement was about more than technical advice. A personal coach who has worked with an athlete over an extended period understands the individual beyond the shooting range, including their habits, temperament and response to pressure.“My personal coach might have seen my tantrums or might have seen a lot,” she says with a laugh. “He has seen various sides of me because I train with him a lot more than I do with my national coach.”She is particularly appreciative of the cooperation between the coaches, describing the atmosphere as one without ego or insecurity. Anthony, she adds, was equally conscious of respecting the national coaching structure.Her introduction to shooting began well before she took up skeet seriously. Growing up around firearms, she was familiar with the sport, and her father, Ratandeep Dhaliwal, encouraged her to learn how to use a weapon. At Mayo College Girls’ School in Ajmer, she participated in open-sight shooting competitions and school-level events.When she turned 13, her father suggested that she explore shotgun shooting. She initially tried trap, but it was an unexpected session at the skeet range that changed her trajectory.During a week at home to prepare for a state competition, her mentor, Amarjang Singh Sidhu, suggested that she try a station of skeet. She hit a couple of targets and immediately found herself drawn to the discipline.“I looked at my dad and said, ‘Papa, I think I want to do skeet.’ He was like, ‘Huh?’” she recalls.Her father discussed the decision with her grandfather, and by the following day, she had a skeet gun.“It turned out to be a great decision,” she says. While she remains close to several trap shooters, skeet is the discipline she finds more engaging. The experience reinforced a lesson she considers fundamental to sporting success: an athlete must enjoy what they do.Behind the medals, however, lies a challenge that is often overlooked: the financial demands of competitive shooting.Shotgun shooting, she explains, can be particularly expensive, making financial stability and institutional support crucial for aspiring athletes. Equipment, training and travel can place a substantial burden on families, while sponsorships often arrive only after an athlete has established a record.Despite having competed at the previous Asian Games, she says she relied on her family to fund her development for years, even while working with internationally accomplished coaches, fitness professionals and sports psychologists.She is grateful for the backing, but is equally conscious of the sacrifices that preceded it. Her father had travelled with her to competitions and camps, both in India and abroad. This year, however, he stepped back from travelling because her grandparents were unwell and needed family support.“I said, for me and for my mental sanity, it’s just better that you are at home with my grandparents. And I’m fine,” she says, drawing on the independence she developed during her years at boarding school.For young shooters, she believes, understanding the financial realities of the sport is as important as recognising their own potential.Parinaaz’s preparation has evolved beyond technique and equipment. Over the past three years, she has worked extensively on fitness and the technical aspects of her shooting, while also consulting a sports psychologist based in the UK.At the elite level, she believes, every component matters. “You cannot leave anything unattended at all,” she said.One incident from the World Cup in Lonato, Italy, illustrates the importance she places on mental preparation. After the first four rounds, she was uncertain about her standing and found herself worrying about the competition. Anthony responded by taking her out for dinner rather than allowing her anxiety to dominate the evening.She was initially concerned about losing sleep ahead of the following morning’s round. Her coach, however, believed that continuing to dwell on the competition would be counterproductive.The evening continued with a walk by the lake and gelato, helping her shift her attention away from the scoreboard and reconnect with the reasons she had taken up shooting.Anthony, she said, believes strongly in maintaining balance and reminding athletes why they compete in the first place.The next day, she shot a perfect round of 25, her best of the competition, which helped her reach a shoot-off.“These are the small things that coaches with experience can teach you,” she said.At the Asian Games, the women's team faced a difficult opening day, but the athletes concentrated on their individual routines rather than becoming distracted by the collective result.Skeet may have a team component, but the discipline demands individual accountability. Each shooter must execute their own process, manage pressure and remain focused on the target in front of them.The team's positive atmosphere helped them persevere, while the men's skeet team also produced a strong finish. India ultimately returned with medals in both the men's and women's team events.For her, the result reflected not only individual ability but also the value of a supportive environment in which athletes and coaches worked towards a common objective.She also believes India's development in skeet coaching needs greater attention. While the country has several accomplished coaches in trap, she sees a relative shortage of experienced specialists in skeet. International coaches, despite their high fees, can offer technical knowledge and an understanding of competitive pressure acquired through years at the highest level.At the same time, she acknowledges that being an accomplished shooter does not automatically make someone an accomplished coach. Coaching, she says, is a discipline in itself.Looking ahead, she intends to continue building on the progress she has made through competition experience, technical refinement and mental preparation. Her latest Asian Games performance is a milestone, but not the end of the journey.For a shooter whose career began with a spontaneous decision at 13, the larger lesson remains remarkably simple: excellence comes from getting the fundamentals right, learning from every competition and finding the people who help you become better.And perhaps that is what defines Parinaaz’s journey best. The targets may be fleeting, but the work behind each shot is anything but.
Article Summary: Parinaaz Dhaliwal won a bronze medal in the women's skeet team event at the Asian Games 2026 at Aichi-Nagoya in Japan. She believes experience, the right coaching environment and an unwavering support system have helped her take significant strides forward. She is grateful for the backing, but equally conscious of the sacrifices that preceded it.

NEW DELHI: In May 2019, before the pandemic had pressed the pause button on the world, Sagar Shah, already an International Master (IM) and one of the most influential voices in today's chess fraternity, wrote a line in his ChessBase column: "Just like Humpy (Koneru) and Harika (Dronavalli) have made the world take note of Indian women's chess over the years, we have a feeling that within a few years Sahithi (Varshini Moogi) and Savitha (Shri Baskar) will also be right up there with the best in women's chess!"More than seven years have passed, and the same line reads less like a prediction and more like a question of legacy, much like asking whether Lamine Yamal could become the next Lionel Messi for Barcelona or whether Carlos Alcaraz could carry the torch of Spanish tennis after Rafael Nadal.Both girls are now 19. At the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand last month, Savitha added a team bronze to her growing list of accolades while also becoming the only Indian to win an individual gold medal at the event Sahithi Varshini, on the other hand, has had a less decorated career so far. The Vizag-born prodigy recently became India’s latest Woman Grandmaster (WGM), a milestone by any measure. But is this the best she can do?"Whatever she has achieved so far, including this one (the WGM title), is not up to her potential. This is just a mere beginning," Lokeswara Moogi Rao, her father and only coach to date, told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interaction.Just last month, Sahithi's third and final WGM norm came at the IM VII Round Robin in Serbia. The 2007-born player finished second with 6/9, recorded a performance rating of 2408, and gained 23 rating points. That completed the requirements.The first two norms came in Hungary. The first was achieved at the Golden Horse IM Round Robin in September 2025, while the second came at the Kanizsa Open in August 2026, where she defeated GM Yeshaayahu Tzidkiya and recorded a performance rating of 2429.On paper, it may look like a clean progression. But the story behind it is much messier.To give a glimpse of how challenging it has been, when Sahithi was six, she caught dengue. She was on a ventilator for a week. She survived, and her family has always seen her recovery as a second life.Long before chess became a part of his life, Lokeswara Moogi Rao, also known as Lokesh in the circuit, had discovered his passion in literature. During his college days, he spent hours immersed in English novels and occasionally tried his hand at writing. Years later, that love for literature would find its way into the name of his second daughter.“Sahithi is similar to Sahitya, which means literature,” Lokesh explained. But the name had another influence, one rooted in music.Lokesh comes from a family with a rich artistic background. His father’s side of the family was involved in theatre, and music was also part of their household. Lokesh himself was a keen singer, winning several prizes at the state level. Among the ragas he particularly admired was Amruthavarshini, whose name he wanted to draw upon for his daughter.His wife, however, felt that literature deserved a place in the name, too. And so, the two influences came together — Sahithi, inspired by literature, and Varshini, drawn from music.“But eventually, she didn’t belong to either of the two and chose the 64 squares,” Lokesh said with a smile. “She made a name for herself in a different domain.”Lokesh was born in a remote village on the edge of Yarada Hills, close enough to the sea that you could see it from the top. But there was no electricity. Before his father secured a job, the family had depended on fishing for a livelihood, as generations on his father’s side had done in a village near Srikakulam district. Walking to the next colony for food took half an hour.He still became a school topper and then a state-ranked student in the engineering entrance. But the family could not afford it. Lokesh's father had retired, and there was no financial backup. He left the course, took a small job after completing a diploma course, and finished an engineering degree by correspondence. Years later, he joined HPCL as an officer.Lokesh was in his early 30s when he started taking chess seriously. He ran a literature club, a small group that exchanged idioms, short stories, and poems by email, trying to sharpen their English in Vizag.One member, Dinesh, a young medical student who lived opposite him, brought a huge chess trophy to the club one day after becoming the Andhra University chess champion. Having learnt that Lokesh had played chess as a child, Dinesh turned up at his house at ten one night with a chessboard.Lokesh's wife Jaya Sri, however, was left unimpressed, asking the two of them to play the game on the balcony.Lokesh was close to winning the first game and then collapsed. The next day Dinesh won two more. The day after, he won two again, and told Lokesh he had found his weakness. "I took it as a challenge," Lokesh recalled. "I wanted to win one game against him. That is how it started."He bought a book from a local shop and began reading in the refinery's control room, where officers sit around digital boards operating the plant. He would sketch positions on paper, then rub them out and redraw. A senior colleague, VS Prasad, caught him doing it and asked if he played chess. Lokesh begged him not to tell the bosses. Prasad took him home instead, to a shelf of 40 or 50 chess books.One was Max Euwe's The Road to Chess Mastery. For a man in love with literature, it certainly felt like a heaven. "It was like a Sherlock Holmes novel kind of a thing," he told this website.Soon, beating Dinesh became a routine. "I won some five to ten games straight away," he shared.Within three months, he made the HPCL team, and within six months of that he was at the national selections for the Petroleum Sports Promotion Board (PSPB), finishing second. He played for the board for roughly seven years, often captaining HPCL.At tournaments, he shared the hall with grandmasters such as Pentala Harikrishna, Shyam Sundar and Koneru Humpy, among others.He was never the strongest player in those rooms. Nevertheless, what he had was an appetite for classical chess. He would take an opening idea from a book, set up the position, and put it to the GMs. They told him he would one day be one of the finest coaches in the country."So that was the foundation," he said, giving us a touch of the philosophy behind Sahithi's approach today.The formal coach within Lokesh became active when her daughters started playing. Despite Sahithi showing early promise, he never set himself a target of IM or GM. What he wanted was a particular kind of game."I always had a very big dream to make her someone like Fischer and Kasparov, not a GM and all," he noted. "I never thought of making IM, GM and then celebrate it. Those moments are important, definitely, in life to cherish and move forward. But my dream was to make her someone like a legend."That ambition shows in how she plays. She goes for sacrifices and attacking positions, and her games grabbed early attention.At 14, she was rated over 2200. Her attacking play drew praise from Scottish Grandmaster, world-famous chess trainer, and author Jacob Aagaard. She also beat women's world champion Mariya Muzychuk."She never fears the opponent. She just plays her style," her coach said.Soon, she had also won a stack of age-group medals, among them Asian and Commonwealth golds.Then came COVID. Sahithi was at her peak, rated highly and seeded at the top of her age groups, and the tournaments stopped. She missed almost three years of competitive chess."You are playing so well, and suddenly, you don't have the option of playing continuously," Lokesh said. "That was really annoying."Leave from work was a problem even before the pandemic. She qualified for a world youth championship (the Cadets tournament) but could not travel. After the lockdowns, Lokesh took long leave and moved the family abroad, reasoning that a rented apartment would cost less than repeated flights. It was a gamble, and he knew it.It also exposed a different problem. Online chess meant every game she played in open tournaments was published, and opponents could prepare against her at the click of a button. A player who loved to surprise people was suddenly easy to study. She tried switching openings from one day to the next, which backfired against stronger opposition.Playing 2300-rated players, he explained, you cannot get away with half-prepared systems. "It did backfire for almost a year," he said.But she came out of it understanding more openings than before. And in 2022 she played at the Chess Olympiad in Chennai, a member of India's C women's team and among the youngest in the squad. "Playing for India is always a special thing," Lokesh told this website.After the Olympiad, the targets slipped away. Sahithi secured a 13th-place finish at the FIDE Women's World Rapid Chess Championship 2023 held in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, which also earned praise from former five-time world champion Viswanathan Anand. She was close to 2300 but not there, and the company could not keep granting leave.The trips abroad were expensive. HPCL contributed around Rs 10 lakh to Sahithi's career, and the Andhra Pradesh government gave a similar amount, but it was not enough."I had to sell an apartment," Lokesh revealed. His wife's gold was pledged. He was running out of options when he reached the most difficult decision almost three years back. "There was only one way. I had to quit my job," he recalled.He resigned and set up a chess academy, which he admits was harder than it sounded. A start in Hyderabad did not work for about ten months, partly because he was away at tournaments with Sahithi.Then, following a heart attack, he had a bypass operation, the heart surgery that forced him to stop for months and reduced both his income and his strength.Around the same time, relatives pressed him to make Sahithi finish class 10. She took nine months away from chess to do it."It sets the morale down," he said of the surgery. "Financially, it also consumes."Jaya Sri was a rock throughout. "I appreciate my wife more than me to be more braver than myself," he said. For a woman who was not earning and had no connection to chess, living with selling property, shifting country, and watching her husband leave his job, he considers it a far harder act of faith than his own.His elder daughter Falguni, now a FIDE arbiter, helped too, paying her own fees and rent by teaching classes.The decision to open the chess academy turned out better than he feared. Back in Visakhapatnam, the academy grew.His student Ajay santhosh Parvathareddy has amassed two GM norms and is now on the verge of beocoming a grand master. Aarav Sinha has collected four IM norms, and others gained hundreds of rating points within months on the European circuit. More than fifteen players now train with him, and he is writing a book on the 2200 level."After surgery, I have had bigger achievements compared to pre-surgery," he remarked.Sahithi was his first student. She remains the one he measures the rest against. But she is not, by his father's account, in the best place mentally."She is a little demotivated, to be frank," Lokesh added. The three lost years still weigh on her. His advice, however, stays the same every time."How you start is not as important as how you end," he tells her. "Whatever you missed in those years, no regrets for that. Just look at what opportunities you have."The plan is to build strength rather than chase a rating. "If you are 2500, you should be able to play like a 2500," he explained. "It should not merely happen with your rating. You should deserve it."The harder obstacle is access. Official events such as the Asian Championships, Commonwealth events and World Juniors come with hotel costs that the family cannot easily meet. Lokesh believes that if Sahithi is given those platforms, results and sponsors will follow. If not, he will keep creating his own opportunities."I'm optimistic that way, rather than regretting not having big sponsors," he acknowledged, thanking Pravaha Foundation for currently sponsoring the chess prodigy in her journey."There are no big names in this journey. No godfathers. You don't require big names to make your stamp. It is your willpower, your passion for the game, your determination, and how you sustain in the difficult phases that take you forward."Perhaps Sagar Shah had got it right all those years ago. Like rice that takes time to cook to perfection over a gentle flame, Sahithi Varshini, too, may need time to come into her own. And when she does, it may well be to carry forward the legacy of those who came before her in chess, sooner rather than later.
Article Summary: Vizag-born prodigy Sahithi Varshini recently became India’s latest Woman Grandmaster (WGM) Her father Lokeswara Moogi Rao, her only coach to date, tells TimesofIndia.com: "This is just a mere beginning"

Article Title: SA vs AUS: Steve Smith cleared of concussion after helmet blow, returns to field in Durban Test
Article Text:
Steve Smith

Smith's concussion history raises concern after helmet blow

Australia close in on victory as South Africa lose two wickets

Poll Vote & Share your view Which aspect of the match has impressed you the most? Steve Smith's resilience Matt Renshaw's batting and bowling performance South Africa's fighting spirit Bowling strategies from both teams 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Former Australia captain Steve Smith has been cleared of concussion and resumed fielding duties on the fifth day of the first Test against South Africa at Kingsmead in Durban on Tuesday, after undergoing a series of clinical assessments following a blow to the helmet.The 37-year-old batter was struck by a short-pitched delivery from Anrich Nortje during Australia's second innings. Smith attempted to duck under the ball but misjudged its trajectory as it failed to rise as much as he expected.Although he continued batting after the incident, scoring 27 off 41 balls before being caught at long-on off Simon Harmer, Smith did not take the field when South Africa began their second innings on Monday. Michael Neser served as his substitute fielder during that session.However, Smith returned to the field on Tuesday morning after being cleared under Cricket Australia's concussion protocols. He was stationed in the slip cordon when South Africa resumed their chase and subsequently took a catch to dismiss Kyle Verreynne off Matt Renshaw's bowling."Steve Smith has undergone a series of clinical assessments over the past 24 hours in accordance with Cricket Australia’s concussion protocols and has been cleared to take the field this morning," Cricket Australia said in a statement.The incident brought back memories of Smith's previous concussion scare during the 2019 Ashes in England, when he was struck on the head by fast bowler Jofra Archer and forced to miss part of a Test match.Smith's return to the field came after medical assessments over the preceding 24 hours, with Australia following the prescribed protocols before allowing the experienced batter to resume his duties.His presence was a boost for Australia as they pushed for victory in the series opener, with South Africa mounting a determined resistance on the final day.South Africa resumed at 102/4 on Tuesday, needing another 319 runs to win. They reached 166/6 by lunch after Australia struck twice to strengthen their grip on the contest.Opener Aiden Markram led the home side's resistance, remaining unbeaten on 69 at the interval alongside Marco Jansen on seven. The pair had to rebuild after Wiaan Mulder's patient 69-run fifth-wicket partnership with Markram ended when Josh Hazlewood had Mulder caught behind by Alex Carey.Part-time spinner Matt Renshaw then dismissed Verreynne, who made just one before edging a reckless shot to Smith at slip.Renshaw has been Australia's standout performer with the bat, having scored 190 in the first innings and 82 in the second, before adding two wickets to his match contribution.Australia needed four more wickets at lunch to seal victory in the opening Test. The second Test of the series is scheduled to begin in Gqeberha on Sunday.
Article Summary: Steve Smith cleared of concussion after blow to the helmet. Former Australia captain was struck by short-pitched delivery from Anrich Nortje. Smith took a catch to dismiss Kyle Verreynne off Matt Renshaw's bowling. Australia needed four more wickets at lunch to seal victory in the opening Test.

Article Title: SA20: Faf du Plessis, Rassie van der Dussen headline auction shortlist
Article Text:
SA20 season 4 delivers USD 406 million boost to South Africa's economy

How things stand ahead of SA20 Auction.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

SA20 Auction Live Streaming

The SA20 Season 5 auction will see 156 cricketers go under the hammer on October 7, with former Joburg Super Kings captain Faf du Plessis Rassie van der Dussen and all-rounder Wiaan Mulder among the leading South African names available.The shortlist was trimmed down from 789 players who initially registered for the auction. Of the 156 players remaining, 95 are South African and 61 are overseas cricketers, with 19 squad places still available across four of the six franchises.Durban's Super Giants and Paarl Royals have already completed their 19-player squads and will not participate in the auction. Joburg Super Kings and MI Cape Town have six slots each to fill, while Pretoria Capitals have five and Sunrisers Eastern Cape have two.JSK and MI Cape Town also have the largest purses available, with $1.24 million and $562,813, respectively. Sunrisers Eastern Cape have $216,699 remaining, while Pretoria Capitals have $88,786.Among the leading South African players in the pool are du Plessis, Mulder, fast bowler Nandre Burger and veteran batter van der Dussen. Du Plessis, who previously led JSK, continues to feature prominently in franchise cricket and recently finished as the leading run-scorer in Europe.The two Under-23 slots are also expected to attract significant interest. Fast bowler Matthew Boast, who commanded the joint-highest bid at the Season 2 auction, is among the players in this category, alongside former South Africa Under-19 captain Jason Rowles.The first four SA20 auctions have produced several significant deals. Tristan Stubbs fetched $554,693 at the inaugural auction, while Dewald Brevis set a new record with a $994,834 deal last season.The auction has also provided a route for several South African players to gain exposure to international franchise cricket, with some subsequently securing further opportunities on the global T20 circuit.The overseas contingent includes former West Indies captain Kieron Pollard, New Zealand pacer Trent Boult, Shimron Hetmyer, Shamar Joseph, Mohammad Nabi, AM Ghazanfar, Jordan Cox, Aneurin Donald, Rehan Ahmed and Richard Gleeson.Several established T20 names are already part of the six franchises, including Jos Buttler, Joe Root, Sam Curran, Sunil Narine, Kane Williamson, Andre Russell, Sherfane Rutherford, Mitchell Marsh and Phil Salt.The auction will be broadcast live on SuperSport at 5pm SAST, JioStar at 8.30pm IST, Sky Sports at 4pm BST, Apex at 7.30pm PKT, Fox Sports at 11pm AEDT and Willow TV at 11am ET. The event will also be streamed live on the SA20 YouTube channel.
Article Summary: The SA20 Season 5 auction will see 156 cricketers go under the hammer on October 7. Former Joburg Super Kings captain Faf du Plessis and all-rounder Wiaan Mulder are among the leading South African names available. Of the 156 players remaining, 95 are South African and 61 are overseas.

Article Title: Ranji Trophy: Andre Siddharth's 81 goes in vain as Rajasthan take 89-run lead
Article Text:
File pic: Andre Siddharth (PTI Photo)

BRIEF SCORES

JAIPUR: Left-arm spinner Ajay Singh Kukna bagged a five-wicket haul to help Rajasthan take a crucial 89-run first innings lead against Tamil Nadu on the penultimate day of the Ranji Trophy match at the Sawai Mansingh Stadium here on Tuesday. Rajasthan ended the eventful Day 3 at 81-4 with an overall lead of 170.Vice-captain Mahipal Lomror (25 batting) and Kartik Sharma (30 batting) were holding fort with an unbeaten fifth-wicket stand of 50 runs after the hosts were tottering at 31/4.Unless a dramatic batting collapse happens on Wednesday morning, it will be a herculean task for the Sai Kishore-led team to pull off a victory from the Elite Group D opening encounter.A disciplined bowling effort backed by some excellent fielding from Rajasthan brought them back in the match. A slice of luck also helped them and put the rivals on the backfoot.Adopting a cautious approach, TN resumed at their overnight score of 167/4 with C Andre Siddharth and Sonu Yadav. Eying a first-innings lead on a flat track, both the batters didn’t take any risk and slowly built the innings. After adding just 36 runs in 24.5 overs, a terrible mix-up between them gifted the hosts the wicket of Yadav.Siddharh tried to repair the damage with Washington Sundar as they put on 61 runs for the sixth wicket.But Kukna turned things around with a gem of a delivery that uprooted the stumps of Siddharth (81). From 264/5, TN lost the rest of the wickets for 10 runs in a span of 4.2 overs in an extraordinary batting collapse.The 29-year-old Kukna (5-51) ended with his seventh five-wicket haul, while left-arm pacer Akash Singh was finally rewarded for his lion-hearted effort with a couple.TN tried to put up a fight with the ball as Sai Kishore picked up two quick wickets with the new ball in Rajasthan’s second innings. Pacers Saravana Kumar and Sonu Yadav took a wicket each and there were hopes of a comeback.However, Kartik-Lomror pair’s gutsy batting at the fag end of the day denied TN any further success.“It was a special effort. I am happy to strike at the crucial juncture to help my team gain a vital lead. We didn’t leak many runs when we were not getting wickets earlier in the day and that ultimately helped us. Manav and I both come from the same place (Sriganganagar) and we always enjoy bowling in tandem.We are in a good position now and can try for an outright win tomorrow,” Kukna told TOI after the day’s play.Rajasthan 363 and 81/4 in 34 overs (Kartik Sharma 30 batting, Mahipal Lomror 25 batting, Karan Lamba 13, Rohan Rajbhar 10; Sai Kishore 2-25, Saravana Kumar 1-4, Sonu Yadav 1-16) vs Tamil Nadu 274 in 98.4 overs (C Andre Siddarth 81, Pradosh Ranjan Paul 58, Narayan Jagadeesan 55, Washington Sundar 26, Baba Indrajith 26; Ajay Singh Kukna 5-51, Akash Singh 2-74).
Article Summary: Rajasthan take crucial 89-run first innings lead against Tamil Nadu. Rajasthan end the eventful Day 3 at 81-4 with an overall lead of 170. Tamil Nadu resumed at their overnight score of 167/4 with C Andre Siddharth and Sonu Yadav.

Article Title: 'My name used without permission': Shikhar Dhawan to take legal action against franchise league
Article Text:
Shikhar Dhawa​n (Credit: Instagram)

A successful career across formats

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former India cricketer Shikhar Dhawan has denied being part of a franchise league, saying the organisers used his name without his knowledge or permission.He also confirmed that his team would take legal action and urged the media and fans not to believe announcements that he has not authorised.In a post on X on October 13, Dhawan clarified his position after finding his name listed as a participant in the tournament.“I have come across my name as a participant in the World T20 Continent Cup. My name has been used by the organisers without my knowledge or permission, and my team will be taking the appropriate legal steps to address this. I request the media and my fans to not report or rely on any unauthorised announcements. Thank you for your continued love and support,” Dhawan added.The former opener made it clear that he had not given permission for his name to be used in connection with the competition. He said his team would take the necessary legal steps to resolve the issue.Dhawan also asked journalists and supporters to verify information before reporting or believing claims about his participation. His statement aims to clear up confusion over his alleged involvement in the tournament.Dhawan was a key member of the Indian cricket team and was particularly successful in One-Day Internationals (ODIs). He played 167 ODIs, scoring 6,793 runs at an average of 44.1, with 17 centuries and 39 half-centuries.In Test cricket, he scored 2,315 runs in 34 matches at an average of 40.6, including seven centuries and five half-centuries.Dhawan also represented India in 68 T20 Internationals, scoring 1,759 runs at an average of 27.9 and recording 11 half-centuries.His statement comes as questions emerge over his reported participation in the World T20 Continent Cup. Dhawan has made it clear that any announcements about his involvement should not be treated as genuine unless they have been authorised by him or his team.
Article Summary: Former India cricketer Shikhar Dhawan has denied being part of a franchise league. He said the organisers used his name without his knowledge or permission. Dhawan also confirmed that his team would take legal action. He urged the media and fans not to believe announcements that he has not authorised.

Article Title: Ranji Trophy: Bengal push for outright win against Delhi
Article Text:
Abishek Porel (Image credit: CAB)

KALYANI: Bengal perhaps missed a chance to put up enough pressure on Delhi by being bowled out for 429 runs just after the lunch interval on Day III of their Elite Group ‘C’ Ranji Trophy match here on Tuesday. However, the visitors still have a job at hand as they lie 88 runs in arrears after being reduced to 101/3 at stumps on the penultimate day.Overnight unbeaten centurion Abishek Porel started off on a positive note by driving pacer Navdeep Saini straight down the ground for a four on the very first ball of the day. However, his unbeaten partner Sudip Gharami looked a bit tentative and was lucky to survive on 131 when Hritik Shokeen dropped an easy catch at deep cover off Saini.But the 229-run fourth-wicket stand between the two came to an end in the very next over when Gharami was trapped in front by pacer Divij Mehra for 133. Shokeen, however, made amends by picking up the prized wicket of Porel when the left-hander offered an easy chance to Sanat Sangwan at forward shot-leg to fall for a well-made 149 runs.Ayush Badoni emerged Delhi’s unlikely wrecker-in-chief when he picked up the hosts’ last three wickets — Akash Deep, Mohammed Shami and Mukesh Kumar — in the second over after lunch to restrict the lead to 189 and return with figures of five for 43.Things could have been worse for Delhi had Sudip Chatterjee held on to a catch offered by opener Sarthak Ranjan in the third over of their second innings being bowled by Shami. For some strange reason Delhi batters went into a shell thereafter as runs completely dried up. In the 19 overs that Delhi faced in the second session of play, only 27 runs were scored.Bengal got back into the act in the last session by picking up two wickets in quick succession. While Mukesh had lefthander Ayush Doseja caught behind by stand-in wicketkeeper Shakib Gandhi, left-arm spinner Pradipta Pramanik had opener Sanat Sangwan clean bowled off the rough for 25.Yash Dhull had to retire hurt after getting hit on the chest by an Akash Deep short rising delivery. However the batter is expected to come out on Wednesday, if required, as he was seen doing some knocking practice at the end of day’s play.Although the wicket is behaving slower, there’s some odd bounce that kept the Bengal camp hopeful. “I still feel we can earn maximum points,” coach Laxmi Ratan Shukla stated.Brief scores: Delhi 240 and 101/3 (S Sangwan 25; Akash Deep 1-15) vs Bengal 429 (A Porel 149, S Gharami 133; A Badoni 5-43).

Article Title: 3rd T20I: Sahibzada Farhan’s 76 in vain as Sri Lanka avoid whitewash againt Pakistan
Article Text:
Player of Pakistan team pose for photograph with T20 series trophy on the of the third T20 cricket match between Pakistan and Sri Lanka, in Rawalpindi, Pakistan, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. (AP Photo/Anjum Naveed)

Kusal Mendis leads Sri Lanka to victory

Farhan shines as Pakistan post 168

Sri Lanka defeated Pakistan by eight wickets in the third and final T20I at Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium on Tuesday, thanks to captain Kusal Mendis’ unbeaten 87. However, Pakistan won the three-match series 2-1 after winning the first two games at the same venue.Chasing 169 runs, Sri Lanka reached 172 for two in just 17.1 overs, securing a comfortable victory. Pakistan had earlier scored 168 for eight in 20 overs.Sri Lanka lost Lahiru Udara early for just one run but recovered through a 59-run partnership between Kusal Mendis and Sineth Jayawardena, who scored 38 off 26 balls.After Jayawardena’s dismissal, Kusal joined Kamindu Mendis to build an unbeaten 98-run partnership that took Sri Lanka home. Kusal smashed nine fours and four sixes in his 48-ball innings, while Kamindu remained unbeaten on 40 off 27 balls.Their partnership ensured Sri Lanka comfortably chased the target and ended the series on a winning note.Earlier, Pakistan captain Sahibzada Farhan led the batting with 76 runs off 47 balls, including seven fours and three sixes. Despite losing wickets regularly, he kept the innings going and recorded his third consecutive half-century of the series.Pakistan slipped to 102 for six before Farhan and Arafat Minhas added 66 runs for the seventh wicket. Minhas scored an unbeaten 34 off 20 balls, helping Pakistan reach 168 for eight.For Sri Lanka, Dasun Shanaka took three wickets for 21 runs, while Nuwan Thushara and Eshan Malinga claimed two wickets each.Although Sri Lanka won the final match, Pakistan secured the series 2-1. Both teams will now prepare for an ODI tri-series featuring England, which begins in Rawalpindi on October 18.

Chasing 169 runs, Sri Lanka reached 172 for two in just 17.1 overs, securing a comfortable victory.

Article Title: Karun Nair's unbeaten 81 keeps Karnataka afloat after top-order collapse against Andhra
Article Text:
Karun Nair

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

VIJAYAWADA: Dropped without explanation from South Zone’s Duleep Trophy XI six weeks ago, Karun Nair has answered in the language he has learnt well lately, runs under pressure. After an unbeaten century in the Dr (Capt) K Thimmappaiah Memorial Tournament recently, the 34-year-old dug Karnataka out of trouble with an unbeaten 81 (130b; 8x4; 2x6) against Andhra in their Ranji Trophy season opener on Tuesday, keeping alive their hopes of salvaging a draw.With Karnataka trailing by 144 runs on the first innings at the ACA Stadium here, the experienced opening pair of Mayank Agarwal (18) and KL Rahul (1) fell cheaply to leave the visitors reeling at 25/2. Karun, however, held his nerve, counterattacked when the opportunity arose and stitched together a 94-run stand with Manvanth Kumar (44) before combining with R Smaran to steer Karnataka to 176/4 in 60 overs, a lead of 32 runs heading into the final day.Having conceded the first-innings lead, Karnataka fought to keep the prospect of a draw and a point alive, reaching 176/4 in 60 overs with a slender 32-run lead heading into the final day.Earlier, Andhra were bowled out for 418 in 121.5 overs, with spinner Shikhar Shetty claiming a six-wicket haul after a long toil.Resuming at 331/4, Andhra lost centurion Seeram Rahul (119) when he was cramped for room by Ritesh Bhatkal (2/109).The teenage debutant added 11 to his overnight score of 108 before departing. Useful contributions from Venkat Sasikanth (39) and Saurabh Kumar (24) took the hosts past 400.Facing a deficit of 144, Mayank and Rahul began cautiously, but Andhra’s astute field placements left the experienced duo with little room even to rotate the strike.Left-arm spinner Saurabh Kumar (3/41) proved particularly effective, using flight and guile to trouble the openers. He nearly had Rahul in the final over before lunch, but an appeal for a catch behind was turned down. The reprieve did little to help the Karnataka batter, who was trapped in front by Saurabh for a laborious one off 20 deliveries. In his next over, the 33-year-old, who moved to Andhra from Uttar Pradesh last season, trapped Mayank to leave Karnataka precariously placed.KV Aneesh (6) was the next to fall, edging Saurabh to skipper Ricky Bhui at first slip. Promoted to No. 3, Manvanth Kumar (44) joined Karun, and the pair set about rebuilding after Manvanth was dropped on seven.Karun eased the pressure with two sixes off Saurabh and Lalith Mohan in successive overs. As Andhra’s bowlers began to stray in line and length, the Karnataka duo grew in confidence. Karun remained a picture of composure, bringing up his half-century off 76 deliveries.Their 94-run fourth-wicket stand ended when Manvanth played back to a Lalith delivery and dragged it onto his stumps.First-innings centurion Smaran then joined Karun, and the pair wore down the Andhra attack with sharp running between the wickets. With Karun holding firm and Smaran providing support, Karnataka moved into a position from which they could realistically save the match.ScoreboardKarnataka (I innings): 274Andhra (I innings; O/N 331/6): SV Rahul lbw Bhatkal 119, Venkat Sasikanth lbw Shikhar 39, Saurabh Kumar c Shrijith b Shikhar 24, Lalith Mohan (not out) 16, Kavuri Saiteja lbw Shikhar 1. Extras: (B-5; LB-5, WD-1; NB-4) 15. Total: (all out; 121.5 overs) 418.Fall of wickets: 7-364, 8-395, 9-416.Bowling: Abhilash Shetty 12-0-49-0, Shikhar Shetty 35.5-2-115-6, Madhav Bajaj 33-4-94-2, Manvanth Kumar 4-0-33-0, Ritesh Bhatkal 35-3-109-2, Karun Nair 2-0-8-0.Karnataka (II innings): Mayank Agarwal lbw Saurabh 18, KL Rahul lbw Saurabh 1, Manvanth Kumar b Lalith 44, KV Aneesh c Bhui b Saurabh 6, Karun Nair (batting) 81, R Smaran (batting) 21. Extras: (LB-5) 5. Total (4 wkts; 60 overs) 176.Fall of wickets: 1-18, 2-25, 3-43, 4-137.Bowling: Kavuri Saiteja 8-1-26-0, Venkat Sasikanth 2-1-4-0, Lalith Mohan 17-1-55-1, Saurabh 18-1-41-3, T Vijay 14-1-43-0, Shaik Rasheed 1-0-2-0
Article Summary: Karun Nair scores unbeaten 81 in Karnataka's Ranji Trophy season opener against Andhra. Karnataka trail by 144 runs on the first innings at the ACA Stadium. Nair stitched together a 94-run stand with Manvanth Kumar (44) before combining with R Smaran to steer Karnataka to 176/4 in 60 overs.

Article Title: How Neeraj Chopra's javelin helped Rohit Yadav win Asian Games bronze
Article Text:
Rohit Yadav (Image credit: X)

NEW DELHI: When Rohit Yadav stepped onto the field in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, for the Asian Games javelin final, he carried more than a piece of sporting equipment. In his hand was a signed javelin belonging to Olympic and world champion Neeraj Chopra — a quiet gesture of support that would accompany him to an international podium.The story began in June, when Yadav struck gold at the National Inter State Senior Athletics Championships in Bhubaneswar with a personal best of 87.05m. Upon returning to his training base in NIS Patiala, he discovered that his preferred javelin had bent, apparently during air transit in its protective PVC tube in the aircraft’s cargo hold.Yadav subsequently competed at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow with a borrowed implement, finishing seventh with 81.56m in cold, windy conditions. With the Asian Games approaching, he faced the prospect of competing without his trusted javelin.“For the Asian Games, I didn’t have my own javelin. My preferred one was damaged and had bent. While coming to Delhi from Patiala for the Indian Athletics Final Series on Sept 10, I spoke to Neeraj bhai,” Yadav told TOI.“We have been in regular touch. I knew he had returned to India for rehabilitation. I told him I didn’t have a javelin of my own for the Asian Games.He immediately came to my rescue and sent me one of his signed javelins through a private taxi service to the Jawaharlal Nehru (JLN) stadium,” he added.Chopra had withdrawn from the remainder of the season, including the Asian Games, to recover from an ankle ligament injury. His absence left India without its two-time defending champion, but his gesture ensured that a fellow Indian thrower had the equipment he needed.There was, however, a catch. Yadav could not use the javelin in Delhi because it had not been registered with the Technical Information Centre (TIC) for inspection. He borrowed another registered implement for the event, then carefully packed Chopra’s gift for Japan.“At the Asian Games, I registered two javelins with the TIC. But I used the one Neeraj bhai gave me. I had a good grip and hold over it, and with that javelin I made the winning throw to secure bronze with 84.35m,” he said.“I will remain thankful to Neeraj bhai. I have kept that javelin with me and will use it in future competitions as well.”After his competition, Rohit listened to Chopra’s congratulatory voice message.“He told me to enjoy the win and savour my first big international medal. He said that when he returns fully fit, we will compete together, and that I have a long way to go.”Back home in Uttar Pradesh’s Jaunpur, Yadav is taking the off-season to spend time with family until Diwali.“I want to earn a Diamond League entry, compete internationally and qualify for the World Championships next year. The ultimate target remains the Los Angeles Olympics,” he added.
Article Summary: Rohit Yadav won bronze at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. Yadav used a signed javelin belonging to Olympic and world champion Neeraj Chopra. Chopra had withdrawn from the remainder of the season to recover from an ankle ligament injury.

Article Title: ‘Olympic gold jeetna hai’: Kumkum Mohod’s big dream after ending Korea’s stranglehold in archery at Asian Games 2026
Article Text:
Kumkum Mohod

TimesofIndia.com

Kumkum Mohod

Manifestation: ‘I had been visualising this for a year’

Kumkum Mohod (AP Photo)

Road to the final: Learning from the best, then beating her

‘My family always supported me’

Gold medallist India's Kumkum Anil Mohod, Ankita Bhakat and Kirti celebrate on the podium during the victory ceremony. (Reuters Photo)

Beyond archery: Drawing, crafts and a dream before sleep

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The ultimate dream: Olympic gold

(Credit: Special arrangement)

NEW DELHI: For years, Kumkum Mohod had watched South Korean archers closely, studying their technique and trying to understand what made them so dominant in recurve archery. She observed their movements, learnt from their approach and looked at the qualities that had made them role models for young Indian archers like her.But when the 17-year-old stood on the shooting line at the Asian Games , just seconds away from releasing her arrow, she had a message for herself: the Koreans were not unbeatable.“Maine match shuru hone se khud ko bol diya tha, woh 10 maarte hain, to mujhe bhi 10 hi maarna hai [I told myself before the match began: they shoot 10s too, so I have to shoot 10s as well],” Asian Games 2026 gold medallist archer Kumkum Mohod toldin an exclusive interview.The 17-year-old made history by winning the women’s individual recurve gold at the Asian Games, beating the Republic of Korea’s Oh Yejin in the final.In doing so, she ended South Korea’s hold on the individual recurve gold at the Games and helped India secure a quota place for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.Before leaving for Aichi-Nagoya, Kumkum had already imagined herself standing on the top of the podium.She had also visualised beating her inspiration, South Korea’s Kang Chaeyoung, whom she eventually defeated in the quarterfinals on her way to the historic gold.Kumkum became the first Indian to win an individual recurve gold at the Asian Games. She also won gold in the women’s recurve team event and silver in the mixed team event with Dhiraj Bommadevara, finishing the Games with three medals.“Until now, no one had managed to do it. But we Indians have done it. We have put the Koreans on a pedestal, as if they are the only ones who can do it and hit those scores. Before the match began, I told myself that they shoot 10s too, and we have to shoot 10s as well,” she said.For Kumkum, the feeling of becoming an Asian Games champion is still sinking in. The young archer said the result did not come as a complete surprise because she had been visualising the moment for a year, even before she stepped onto the field in Japan.For a year leading up to the Asian Games, she repeated the same words five times before going to sleep: “Kumkum, Asian Games gold jeetna hai” (Kumkum, you have to win Asian Games gold). She would then say “Hare Krishna”, reflecting her devotion to Lord Krishna.Her belief was tested against some of the world's best archers. Kumkum defeated South Korea’s reigning world champion and Olympic medallist Kang Chaeyoung 6-3 in the quarterfinals before beating China’s Zhu Jingyi 6-2 in the semifinals.In the final, she held her nerve against South Korea’s Oh Yejin. The contest ended 5-5 after five sets, forcing a shoot-off. Oh shot an eight, while Kumkum hit a 10 to seal the gold medal.Kumkum had been trailing during the match and needed to win the fifth set to stay in contention. She responded by shooting a perfect 30 to force the shoot-off before producing the decisive 10.“The final went really well. I was trailing, but I remained strong. I believed in myself and knew I could do it because I had been visualising this for the past year. I kept imagining that I would face Kang in a match and that it would be a final,” Kumkum said.When Oh shot an eight in the shoot-off, Kumkum had to focus on her own shot rather than the possibility of winning. She knew she had to deliver, regardless of what her opponent had scored.“I had made up my mind that day that I had to prove myself. My first thought was, ‘Kumkum, you still have to shoot a good shot.’ Even if she had shot a 10, I was very confident at that moment,” she said.“I enjoyed that moment while shooting. There is always some pressure, but I tried to reduce it. Anyone who says there is no pressure is absolutely wrong. Sport is about nerves and thrilling moments. There is always adrenaline, and you have to overcome it. The person who manages to do that wins,” she said.Kumkum's journey to the gold medal included victories over some of the world's leading archers. But one of the most memorable moments for her was beating Kang, an archer she had admired and learnt from since the beginning of her career.Kang had been Kumkum's inspiration because of her technique, focus, composure and ability to deliver under pressure. Kumkum paid particular attention to her release and follow-through, as well as the way she maintained her technique in crucial moments.At the Asian Games, however, the young Indian found herself competing against the very archer she had looked up to for years - and came out on top.“Kang’s shooting technique is very good. Her release is excellent, and she does not drop her bow after the follow-through. Her shooting is very strong,” Kumkum said.So, the victory carried special meaning. After the match, Kumkum exchanged a high-five with her opponent and told her, “Good shooting, good shooting.”Kang smiled and congratulated her.“I have learnt a lot from her, and I was happy. She is a legend of the sport. She has made her country proud by winning medals, and now I have done the same. I am proud that I have made my country proud,” Kumkum said.Behind Kumkum’s success is a family that continued to believe in her, even when her performances were not going as planned.Her father, Anil Mohod, runs a business making sweet boxes. As Kumkum was good at academics, her father initially wanted her to focus on her studies. But when he saw her growing interest in archery, her family supported her sporting ambitions while ensuring that she did not neglect her education.Kumkum is the couple’s only child and is currently in Class 12.“I joined archery, and within six months, I won a medal. After that, I learnt about the Olympics and understood what the sport could lead to. I also learnt that India had not won a medal in this event. My interest grew, and I started working harder,” she said.Her family’s faith in her remained strong even during difficult periods.“When I was not doing well, my family told me that I could do it. They have supported me a lot, and I never faced any problems because of them,” she said.Now, following her historic achievement, the Mohod household has been welcoming a steady stream of visitors. Neighbours, friends, relatives, sports associations and fellow sportspersons have been arriving to congratulate the family.Kumkum said the celebrations have kept everyone busy, with little time to rest.“It feels like a wedding atmosphere at home. People keep coming and going, and we are hardly getting any sleep. All thanks to Krishna ji,” she said.Away from the archery range, Kumkum enjoys spending time with a paintbrush and a colour palette. Drawing and craftwork are among her favourite hobbies, giving her a break from the demands of training and competition.“I like drawing and crafting. I also enjoy making things with my hands,” she said.She also enjoys watching television shows and films. Her favourites include Taarak Mehta Ka Ooltah Chashmah and sports-based films such as Dangal, Mary Kom, Ghoomer and Bhaag Milkha Bhaag.Unlike many teenagers, Kumkum has never had Facebook or Instagram accounts. She also disabled YouTube a few months before the Asian Games. Drawing, craftwork and reading are among the activities she enjoys away from the range.“I never had Facebook or Instagram. I also disabled YouTube a few months before the Asian Games. My crafts, drawing and reading books help me a lot,” she said.Kumkum has already achieved a major milestone by winning three medals at the Asian Games and helping India secure a quota place for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. But she has a bigger dream — winning India's first Olympic gold medal in archery.The words she repeated before going to sleep for a year - “Kumkum, Asian Games gold jeetna hai” - now reflect a new ambition: “Kumkum, Olympic gold jeetna hai.”At home, a small message on the wall serves as a reminder of what she wants to achieve.“LA 2028 gold is the target. That is the dream. I do not want to think too far ahead just yet, but that is the target. I will work hard for it and strengthen myself mentally,” Kumkum signed off.
Article Summary: Kumkum Mohod is the first Indian to win an individual recurve gold at the Asian Games. The 17-year-old made history by beating the Republic of Korea’s Oh Yejin in the final. She also won gold in the women's recurvies team event and silver in the mixed team event.

Article Title: Historic Olympic quota, multiple medals — but no salary: India’s compound archery coach unhappy over payment delay
Article Text:
Sahil Jadhav, left, and Chikitha Taniparthi, right, celebrate with coach Dave Cousins after winning the compound mixed team archery gold. (PTI Photo)

A historic breakthrough, but a salary dispute

Sahil Jadhav and Chikitha Taniparthi with team coach Dave Cousins during the Asian Games. (PTI Photo)

AAI, SAI say payment will be cleared soon

Building towards LA 2028
