NEW DELHI: India's compound archers made history at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games by becoming the first nation to secure an Olympic quota in the discipline. But while the team celebrated a landmark achievement and a rich medal haul, the foreign coach who helped guide them to success was left unhappy over a salary delay stretching beyond three months.American Dave Cousins, appointed as India's chief compound archery coach in May, is learnt to have threatened to quit and leave the country if his pending dues were not cleared, as per a PTI report.The development has raised questions about the support extended to a coach who has already delivered significant results as India builds towards the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. However, the Archery Association of India (AAI) and the Sports Authority of India (SAI) have acknowledged the delay, attributing it to a technical issue and saying the matter has now been resolved, with the payment expected to be cleared shortly."He has spoken to some officials and said if the dues are not cleared he's leaving home. He's really unhappy with the way he's been treated for three months... he's not been paid so far," sources told PTI.Cousins helped India win three gold medals and a bronze in compound archery at the Asian Games, contributing to the country's overall haul of five gold, two silver and two bronze across recurve and compound events.The biggest breakthrough came in the mixed-team event, where the relatively unfancied Indian pair of Sahil Jadhav and Chikitha Taniparthi stunned South Korea in a shoot-off after the final was tied 157-157 over four ends.The victory secured India its first-ever Olympic quota in compound archery, a discipline that will feature a mixed-team event at the 2028 Los Angeles Games.Cousins had taken charge of India's compound programme with the responsibility of building a competitive unit for the Olympics. His results at the Asian Games came with a group that had faced questions about its ability to deliver at the highest level.The American had also guided 18-year-old Prithika Pradeep to her maiden World Cup bronze at the Madrid stage in Spain.Reflecting on India's Asian Games campaign, Cousins had stressed that preparation, rather than medal predictions, was the team's priority."The only thing we were willing to commit to is that our athletes would go prepared and that they would execute the process as best they could," he had said."When the training is right, the preparation is right and the ecosystem is right, these are the results you get. We're exceptionally happy to clinch the first-ever compound archery spot for the Olympic Games. That's a huge thing for us right now."AAI treasurer Dr Joris Paulose Ummacheril acknowledged the delay but said the issue had been resolved and the payment would be made shortly."There was some issue with the Sports Authority of India (SAI), so the payment got delayed. But it has all been worked out, and it will be paid within two days," Joris told PTI.An SAI official in New Delhi also attributed the delay to a technical problem involving the bank, adding that the matter was being processed."We have already spoken to him and assured him that the payment is under process. It got delayed because of a technical issue with the bank, and it should be done within a couple of days," the official said.The assurances suggest that the dispute could be resolved soon, although the episode has highlighted the administrative challenges that can undermine the momentum generated by sporting success.Cousins, 49, is a former world No. 1 who won World Archery Championship titles in 1999 and 2003. His appointment in May followed the departure of Sergio Pagni, under whom India swept all five archery gold medals at the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou.Meanwhile, the federation is also in talks with South Korean coach Park Chae-soon to take charge of India's recurve programme ahead of LA 2028. Park, who coached South Korea's women's team at the London 2012 Olympics and men's team at Rio 2016, is expected to join by December.With India's archers building momentum towards the next Olympics, Cousins' contribution has already produced a landmark result in compound archery. The historic quota and multiple Asian Games medals have strengthened India's prospects in a discipline making its Olympic debut in Los Angeles.
Article Summary: India's compound archers made history at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games by becoming the first nation to secure an Olympic quota in the discipline. Coach Dave Cousins is learnt to have threatened to quit and leave the country if his pending dues were not cleared. The development has raised questions about the support extended to a coach who has already delivered significant results as India builds towards the 2028 Olympics.

Article Title: ‘I was a daughter of Himachal’: Ritu Negi’s heartbreak after home state drops Asian Games gold medallist from Rs 1 crore reward list

‘Why is Himachal Pradesh behaving this way at this stage of my career?’

Former India captain Ritu Negi has represented the country at three consecutive Asian Games, won two gold medals and a silver, and led the women's kabaddi team to the top of the podium at the 2023 edition in Hangzhou. Yet, after being part of India's gold-medal-winning squad again at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, the Arjuna Awardee has found herself at the centre of an unexpected controversy in her home state of Himachal Pradesh.Negi's name was missing from the state's list of athletes announced for a cash reward of Rs 1 crore following India's women's kabaddi triumph in Japan. The decision has left the veteran player disappointed and raised questions about whether an accomplished sportsperson should lose recognition from her home state simply because she is married in another state.Negi hails from the Shillai region of Sirmaur district but is married in Panipat, Haryana. The omission has been particularly difficult to understand because she received a cash reward from Himachal Pradesh after India's women's kabaddi team won gold at the 2023 Asian Games, when she was the captain.This time, however, her name was left out while three other players from the state were included in the reward list."Until a week ago, I was a daughter of Himachal and the CM shared a congratulatory message on Facebook, while former CM Jairam Thakur and Member of Parliament Anurag Thakur had called to congratulate me," Negi told the media while expressing her displeasure."I simply cannot understand what changed so suddenly two days ago."The decision to exclude Negi has struck a particularly sensitive chord because of her long association with Indian kabaddi and her contribution to the state's sporting reputation.The veteran has represented India at three consecutive Asian Games, winning two gold medals and a silver. She captained the women's team to gold at Hangzhou in 2023 and remained part of the squad that successfully defended the title in Japan.India edged past Iran 37-34 in a tense final at the Aichi-Nagoya Games, holding on to its advantage in the closing stages to secure another Asian Games gold.The achievement should have been another moment of pride for the player and her home state. Instead, the omission from the reward list has left Negi questioning the recognition being extended to her.She pointed out that although she is employed by Indian Railways , she has consistently represented Himachal Pradesh, rather than Haryana, in domestic competitions."Why Himachal Pradesh is behaving in such a way at this stage of my career?" she asked.For Negi, the issue goes beyond the financial incentive. It is about recognition for years of representing India and maintaining her sporting association with the state from which she hails.Negi's father, Bhavan Singh Negi, has also questioned the decision, asking whether a daughter ceases to belong to her home state simply because she gets married elsewhere.Speaking from Shillai in Sirmaur district, he pointed out that his daughter had received a cash reward from the Himachal government after the 2023 Asian Games, despite being married in Haryana.That precedent has made the latest omission even harder for the family to comprehend. They believe marriage should not erase an athlete's roots or diminish her contribution to the state she continues to represent in domestic competitions.The controversy has since drawn reactions from political leaders and people associated with sports in Himachal Pradesh.The debate has consequently become about more than a reward announced after a sporting achievement. It has raised questions about how states recognise athletes who continue to bring them distinction despite changes in their personal circumstances.The controversy emerged after Himachal Pradesh Chief Minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu announced a cash reward of Rs 1 crore each for three players from the state who were part of India's women's kabaddi gold-medal-winning squad at the Aichi-Nagoya Games.The recipients were Pushpa Rana, Jyoti Thakur and Bhawna Thakur. Indian women's cricket player Renuka Thakur was also announced as a recipient of Rs 1 crore in recognition of her achievements.The announcement followed an earlier disagreement over the amount offered to the kabaddi players. Initially, the three players had been informed that they would receive Rs 33 lakh each, a figure they felt was below their entitlement under the state's sports policy. They subsequently met Sukhu to raise their concerns over the cash incentives and employment opportunities.Pushpa Rana said the players were disappointed by the original announcement."Look, we were very disappointed because according to the sports policy, we were not being given the amount that was due to us. So literally, anyone would be disappointed," she told IANS.Following the meeting, the Chief Minister assured the players that the reward would be increased to Rs 1 crore each. The state government also announced government employment for the three kabaddi players, with options in the police department or the Youth Services and Sports Department.While the revised announcement addressed the players' concerns over the amount, Negi's omission from the list brought a fresh controversy into focus.The Himachal Pradesh government has not publicly provided a definitive explanation for why Negi's name was removed from the list.Sports Minister Yadvinder Goma said he was unaware of the reason behind the change and would examine the file before discussing the matter with the Chief Minister.Meanwhile, sources in the state government indicated that officials were monitoring the Haryana government's position on the matter. They suggested that Himachal Pradesh could consider a decision later, particularly since Haryana had not yet announced a cash award for Negi.The sources also indicated that her employment with Indian Railways was not a factor in the matter.The distinction is important because Negi has maintained that she has continued to represent Himachal Pradesh in domestic competitions despite her marriage and employment outside the state.Whether the government ultimately revises its list remains to be seen. For now, the Sports Minister's assurance that he will review the matter offers a possible route towards resolving the dispute.For Negi, the timing of the controversy is especially poignant.At the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou, she captained the women's kabaddi side to gold and received recognition from her home state. At the Aichi-Nagoya Games, she again stood among the Indian players who helped defend the title, contributing to a campaign that ended with another gold medal for the country.Her sporting journey has been built around representing India at the highest level while continuing to identify with Himachal Pradesh. The latest controversy has placed that connection under an uncomfortable spotlight.Negi's case also highlights a broader challenge in Indian sport: ensuring that recognition for athletes reflects their achievements and contributions, rather than becoming entangled in questions about residence, marriage or administrative eligibility.The government has yet to make its final position clear, and the possibility of reconsideration remains open. Until then, the former India captain's disappointment stands as a reminder that recognition can matter as much as the reward itself.

Article Title: ‘I’m not going to the military’: What is military exemption? Why South Korea weighs cuts after Asian Games backlash
Article Text:
South Korean football team after winning the Asian Games gold medal. (Pic credit: X)

What is South Korea's military exemption for athletes?

Why is South Korea considering cuts now?

History of the athlete exemption

Who else benefited at the Asian Games?

Will South Korea abolish military exemptions for athletes?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

South Korea is reconsidering a decades-old military service benefit for elite athletes after controversial comments by Asian Games gold medallists triggered a fresh public debate over whether sporting success should continue to qualify some young men for an alternative to the country's compulsory military service.The controversy erupted after South Korea won the men's football gold medal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, beating Japan 1-0 in the final on Saturday. Several players came under fire for comments and social-media activity related to the military benefit that came with their gold medal.Captain Lee Gi-hyuk, winger Yang Min-hyuk and forward Park Seung-soo all faced criticism. Lee held up his gold medal and said, “I’m not going to the military,” while Yang said the military-service benefit had been his main motivation during the tournament. Park posted a photograph of himself wearing a cap associated with people who have completed their mandatory military service.All three subsequently apologised. But the episode reignited a much bigger question in South Korea: why should athletes receive special treatment when most young men are required to serve?The government is now reviewing the system.Culture, Sports and Tourism Minister Chae Hwi-young said Wednesday that his ministry would consult the sports and arts communities, the Defence Ministry and the Military Manpower Administration as it considers comprehensive measures.The Defence Ministry has gone further. It said it was considering either scaling back or abolishing supplementary military service for artists and athletes, while Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul said the ministry's goal was to gradually reduce the exemptions and ultimately abolish them.South Korea has a mandatory military-service system under which able-bodied men generally have to complete between 18 and 21 months of service.But athletes who achieve specified international sporting results can receive an alternative-service benefit instead of serving the standard term. Under the current rules, athletes who win an Olympic medal or an Asian Games gold medal qualify for the arrangement.The term “military exemption” is widely used, but it can be slightly misleading.The athletes are not simply released from every military-related obligation. Those who qualify are assigned to supplementary service. They undergo three weeks of basic military training and then have to complete 544 hours of community service over 34 months.For elite athletes, however, the difference is significant.Instead of spending 18 to 21 months in regular military service, they can continue training and competing while completing their alternative-service obligations. That can be particularly important for footballers, golfers, baseball players and other professionals whose careers can be affected by a long interruption during their peak years.The benefit can also have implications for athletes playing overseas because avoiding a lengthy interruption can allow them to maintain their club careers and development.At the 2026 Asian Games, 20 of South Korea's 23 men's football players became eligible for the benefit after the 1-0 victory over Japan.The immediate trigger is the backlash over the footballers' comments.Yang Min-hyuk was criticised after saying the medal and championship were not important to him and that he had played with the military-service benefit in mind.Lee's “I’m not going to the military” remark also drew criticism, while Park's photograph wearing a military discharge-style cap became another focus of the controversy.The players later apologised, with Lee saying he should have considered the weight of his words and Yang explaining that the military benefit was one of several motivations that had been expressed poorly.But the government response suggests the controversy is being viewed as part of a wider problem rather than as an isolated incident.The Defence Ministry said it would consider fairness among people subject to mandatory service, the declining number of people available for military service and public consensus when deciding the future of the supplementary-service system.South Korea's declining birth rate means the pool of young men available for military service is shrinking. That demographic pressure has added importance to the question of who can receive alternative arrangements.There is also a fairness argument. While athletes can qualify through sporting achievements, other high-profile South Koreans have had to complete military service.The issue has been particularly sensitive in the entertainment industry because members of BTS, one of South Korea's biggest cultural exports, completed their military obligations rather than receiving an athlete-style exemption.The comparison has repeatedly featured in the debate over whether exceptional achievements in sport, popular culture or other fields should qualify someone for special treatment.The system dates back to 1973, when South Korea introduced the special arrangement for athletes and artists as part of a broader effort to develop elite talent and enhance the country's international standing.Over the decades, the policy became particularly important in sports such as football and baseball, where military service could interrupt the careers of players competing at home and overseas.The Asian Games has traditionally been especially significant because gold, rather than simply any medal, is required for athletes to qualify.That has sometimes produced unusual incentives around the tournament. For South Korea's football and baseball players, an Asian Games gold medal can effectively remove the possibility of a lengthy interruption to their professional careers.The policy has also generated controversy before.Debates intensified after South Korea's run to the 2002 World Cup semi-finals led to a special exemption arrangement for members of that squad, although the World Cup was later removed from the exemption rules.The system has continued to face questions over whether sporting achievement should be sufficient grounds for an alternative to compulsory service.The football players were not the only South Koreans to qualify.South Korea's baseball players earned the benefit after defeating Japan 3-1 in the final. Gold medallists in esports also qualified under the rules.Golfer Tom Kim won the men's individual gold after travelling to Japan following the Presidents Cup. His response to the military-service issue was markedly different from the comments that triggered the controversy.“I’m more proud that I’m able to bring a medal for my country,” Kim said.The episode therefore illustrates the two sides of the current debate: the argument that sporting success can justify an alternative service arrangement for athletes representing South Korea, and the growing concern that such benefits may be difficult to reconcile with the principle that military service should be shared fairly.There is no immediate abolition, but the government is now openly discussing major changes.The Defence Ministry said it plans to reflect a reduction or abolition of supplementary service for artists and athletes in its defence-reform plans. Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul subsequently said the ministry's goal was to gradually scale back the system and ultimately abolish it.The Culture Ministry is separately reviewing the system and plans to consult athletes, artists, defence officials and the Military Manpower Administration before deciding on comprehensive measures.That means the controversy surrounding the Asian Games footballers could have consequences well beyond their apologies.A system that has existed for more than five decades is now facing a renewed examination at a time when South Korea is dealing with a shrinking pool of young men available for military service and changing public expectations about fairness.For athletes, the debate is ultimately about more than a medal. An Asian Games gold can currently mean the difference between an 18-to-21-month interruption and a much less disruptive alternative-service arrangement.For the government, the question is whether that distinction remains justified — and whether a benefit created more than 50 years ago still fits the realities of modern South Korea.
Article Summary: South Korea is reconsidering a decades-old military service benefit for elite athletes. Controversy erupted after South Korea won the men's football gold medal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, beating Japan 1-0 in the final on Saturday. Several players came under fire for comments and social-media activity related to the military benefit.

India’s 21-gold campaign at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games has thrown up an interesting set of numbers: champions who reached the continental podium despite receiving relatively modest targeted financial assistance under the govt’s elite-athlete programmes.Their stories do not diminish the broader support extended to Indian sport. Instead, they underline how performances can sometimes run ahead of the funding pipelines designed to identify and back medal prospects.The clearest example is 17-year-old archer Kumkum Mohod. A recently-inducted Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS) athlete for the Aich-Nagoya preparatory cycle, Kumkum became the first Indian woman to win an individual recurve gold at the Games, defeating South Korea’s Oh Yejin 6-5 after a shoot-off. She also won gold in the women’s recurve team event and silver in mixed team, ending the campaign with three medals and securing India an LA Olympics quota.The funding support extended to her puts her targeted assistance at just Rs 50,000. That is a striking figure against the scale of her achievement, even though her preparation also benefited from the budget allocated to the respective national sports federations (NSFs) under the Annual Calendar for Training and Competition (ACTC).The same pattern is visible in compound archery. Sahil Rajesh Jadhav, who helped India win mixed team gold with Chikitha Taniparthi and also contributed to the men’s team gold, received Rs 50,000 under TOPS during the Games cycle. His top podium finish also delivered India an Olympic quota in compound archery.Kushal Dalal and Thirumuru Ganesh Maniratnam, members of India’s men’s compound team that defeated China for gold, also received only Rs 50,000 each under TOPS during the cycle. Yet the trio of Dalal, Ganesh and Jadhav produced one of India’s five archery gold medals at the Games.The contrast becomes sharper when placed alongside athletes receiving substantially larger targeted allocations. Boxer Ankush Panghal, for instance, received Rs 75,000 under TOPS, while his other gold partners in boxing Lovlina Borgohain and Parveen Hooda received Rs 22.97 lakh and Rs 8.59 lakh assistance, respectively, during the Games cycle.These figures show that support was available at markedly different levels depending on an athlete’s classification, requirements, and timing within the system.Similarly, in sailing, Harshita Tomar and Shital Verma secured the bronze medal in the women’s skiff, with both athletes not being part of the TOPS programme. Also, in the same sport, sailors Manu Francis and Prince Noble won silver in the men’s skiff, but both were not part of either TOPS Core or Development group. Boxer Kapil Pokhariya, too, wasn't part of the TOPS.In shooting, the trio of Manisha Keer, Neeru Dhanda and Aashima Ahlawat won the silver medal in Trap women's team event, with Manisha receiving no TOPS assistance while Neeru, a TOPS Development athlete, getting Rs one lakh. In athletics, silver-wining javelin thrower Yashvir Singh wasn't part of the TOPS funding and largely prepared through the ACTC budget. In kurash, bronze-winner Pincky Balhara, competing in the -78 kg event, received Rs 75,000 under the TAGG scheme during the Games cycle.Kumkum Mohod (Rs 50,000), Sahil Jadhav (Rs 50,000), Kushal Dalal (Rs 50,000), Thirumuru Maniratnam (Rs 50,000),Ankush (Rs 75,000), Kapil Pokhariya (not covered under TOPS);Neeru Dhanda (Rs 1,00,000),Pincky Balhara (Rs 75,000),Seema (Rs 25,000), Baranica Elangoan and Yashvir Singh (both not covered under TOPS).

The funding support extended to her puts her targeted assistance at just Rs 50,000. The contrast becomes sharper when placed alongside athletes receiving substantially larger targeted allocations.

NEW DELHI: Lovlina Borgohain ’s Asian Games gold was not just a medal upgrade from silver in the last edition. It was the latest marker in a 15-year career that has taken the Assam boxer through Olympic success, injuries, difficult phases and a mentally demanding Paris 2024 campaign.At the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Borgohain finally changed the colour of her Asian Games medal, defeating China’s Bao Ziyi 5-0 in the women’s 75kg final. The victory, on her 29th birthday, made her only the second Indian woman after MC Mary Kom to win boxing gold at the Asian Games -- 12 years after Kom’s 2014 triumph.For Borgohain, however, the gold's significance went beyond the history books.“It’s still difficult to get out of this moment. I still have the gold medal in my hand," said a beaming Borgohain while lifting the gold medal next to her face. "It’s a very special moment for me. I can’t express how I feel,” she continued as she spoke to TimesofIndia.com upon returning from Japan.Borgohain had finished with silver at the 2022 Hangzhou Asian Games, losing to China’s Li Qian in the final. Three years later, she returned to the continental stage determined to go one step further.Her path to the gold in Nagoya was not straightforward. She began with a 5-0 quarter-final win over South Korea’s Seong Su-yeon before edging Kazakhstan’s reigning 70kg world champion Natalya Bogdanova 3-2 in a closely fought semi-final.She then produced a 5-0 win over Ziyi in the final.The contrast with Hangzhou made the medal particularly meaningful.“Every event is very important. We believe that the Asian Games medal is the highest after the Olympics. I think this medal is shining amidst all the medals. The colour has changed. This medal means a lot to me,” Borgohain said.“I got a silver medal in the last Asian Games and this time I got a gold medal. This is why it is so special. And to do it on my birthday is extra special.”The victory also continued a curious connection between Borgohain and Japan. Five years ago, Tokyo had brought her an Olympic bronze medal — the breakthrough that changed the trajectory of her career.“I was very excited because I was going to Japan again. I had won a medal in (the) 2020 Olympics in Japan, and my life changed because of that,” she said.“I had a positive mindset before leaving India. I wanted to make it the best tournament of my life. I knew that I could do it because Japan is lucky for me.”The gold also offered a reminder of Borgohain’s ability to rebuild.Her career has not followed a straight line since the Tokyo Olympics. Injuries, changes in form and the disappointment of the Paris Olympics tested her, while the pressure that came with becoming an Olympic medallist added another layer to the challenge.Borgohain does not, however, see the Asian Games gold as something that has fundamentally changed her.“I don’t think I am looking at myself differently because of this medal. I have won and lost a lot of medals. People’s perspective changes because of the medal. But I am always the same in my own eyes,” she said.“My perspective has not changed because of the medal. When I lose, my self-belief remains the same. Sometimes I am confident, and sometimes I am down. But I am the same person that I was before.”That mindset became particularly important after Paris 2024, when she failed to reach the medal rounds. Borgohain describes the period as one of the most difficult phases of her career.“I have a 15-year journey. Every time I go to a competition, my mindset is different. When we play, we reach the medal. It is not easy to recover from a tough period. The 2024 Paris Olympics wasn’t an easy period for me mentally,” she said.“But I think everything is a game of the mind. It depends on how we look at it. If we take tough things easy, it becomes easy. If we take easy things hard, it becomes hard. I think that helped me a lot to keep myself calm and relaxed.”The Asian Games victory has also given Borgohain a more direct route towards the next stage of her career. The gold means she qualifies for the World Championships, rather than having to go through the national selection route. A strong performance there could also put her on the road to another Olympic qualification campaign.“It matters a lot for an athlete because of this medal I am qualifying for the World Championships. I am getting a good treat otherwise I would have to play the Nationals and follow the same process,” she said.“So that is a big advantage of the medal, and it boosts my confidence that I can do better. If I do well there, then I can qualify for the Olympics also.”For now, though, Borgohain is resisting the temptation to look too far ahead.“There is a lot of planning. But not everything is the same. I am living in the present. I don’t know what will happen tomorrow. I will try to live like this. It makes me feel good. I will try to live like this.”Borgohain’s gold was part of a strong boxing campaign for India at the Asian Games. India finished the competition with six boxing medals, including three golds, with Parveen Hooda and Ankush Panghal also winning their respective finals.Some months back, Indian boxers had returned with 10 medals at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, including seven golds. No country had won more golds in boxing at a single edition of the CWG. It was also India's largest haul in the sport in a CWG.For Borgohain, the improvement reflects a broader change in the mentality of Indian boxers.“We had a very good performance. Both men and women did very well. Everyone knows the results of the Commonwealth Games. The results of the Commonwealth Games changed the results of Indian Boxing,” she said.“In the Asian Games, our Indian team came out on top. I think our athletes are very strong. Their mentality is very good. We used to think that we would not be able to do it. But now our young athletes have the mindset that ‘we have to do it’.”She also pointed to the support structure around the team, including government backing and the environment created by the coaching staff led by Santiago Nieva.“The support of the government matters a lot. They don’t let us down. We are getting good competition. The environment of our foreign coaches, led by Santiago (Nieva), is very positive. That is why we are getting good results.”For Borgohain, then, the Asian Games gold is both an ending and a beginning — the end of a 12-year wait since Mary Kom’s historic gold and the completion of a personal journey from Hangzhou silver to Nagoya gold.But she is not treating it as a destination. The next target can wait. For now, she is content to live in the moment — with the gold medal still in her hand.
Article Summary: Boxer Lovlina Borgohain won gold at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya. She beat China's Bao Ziyi 5-0 in the women's 75kg final. The victory, on her 29th birthday, made her only the second Indian woman after Mary Kom to win boxing gold.

CHENNAI: With three medals and newfound recognition, Vithya Ramraj returned home from the Asian Games with plenty to celebrate. People at petrol bunks, airports and bus stands have started recognizing her, but it has left the 28-year old, who broke P T Usha’s 400 metre 42-year-old hurdles record, slightly surprised.“People are recognising me now and I’m happy athletics is growing. I’m also thinking about the recognition I am getting. Is it because of the relay medals or because I broke the record? Why have I become famous? That is one constant thing on my mind. I’m still far away from reaching world standards, and my coach was not happy with the timing.“Personally, I didn’t get the satisfaction even though people celebrated. I think of how Neeraj Chopra is celebrated, and if I reach his level, then more people will know me,” Vithya told TOI.What worked for Vithya in 400m hurdles was that she brought down her stride count from 17 to 16 between hurdles 5 and 6.“In the bend from the fifth to the sixth hurdle, I used to take 17 strides, but I have now reduced it to 16. We have been working on it since Nov last year. That helped me going into the home stretch.”Going into the Asian Games, Vithya did not dip below 56 seconds even once this season. While she bagged gold at the Federation Cup and Inter-state athletics meet, her coach Nehpal Singh, who has been a strong source of support, was not satisfied with the medals.“My coach told me, ‘Did I train you to run 56 seconds? What performance have you put in?’”What Vithya felt helped her in the run-up to the Asian Games was the training stints she had in Poland and the Czech Republic with Nehpal.“I used to sleep for 10 hours for three months during the stint abroad, but in India, I used to sleep only for 7-8 hours. In India, I cannot train at 10 am due to the climate, but the sleep cycle in Poland helped me. In India, I train from 5:30am to 8:30am,” she said.

NEW DELHI: Two years ago, Sujeet Kalkal was stranded at Dubai International Airport, watching his Olympic dream slip away with every passing hour.On his way to Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, for the Asian Olympic Qualifying Tournament, Kalkal was stuck in Dubai for three days after floods disrupted his travel plans. By the time a flight was arranged, it was too late. He could not reach Bishkek in time, and with it went his chance to qualify for the Paris Olympics.Two years later, the disappointment of Dubai has been replaced by an Asian Games gold. Kalkal, the world No. 2 in the men's 65kg category, fought back from 2-9 down against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev in the final to win 10-9, ending India's eight-year wait for a wrestling gold at the Games.The comeback was symbolic of what Kalkal's career has looked like since that Olympic setback. He has had to rebuild, compete through the disappointment and find a way back to the biggest stages. On Sunday, he did that with an Asian Games title.When the final whistle came, Kalkal folded his hands, looked up and thanked God. He then took a lap of the arena with the Indian tricolour draped around his shoulders, tears and a broad smile.For a wrestler who had once been denied even the chance to fight for an Olympic place, the moment carried a little more weight than an Asian Games gold."This gold means a lot to me. Not just because it is an Asian Games gold, but because there is so much behind this medal. The last few years have had many ups and downs, and I missed a few opportunities, but I never lost belief in myself," Kalkal told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview on his way back to Imlota village in Bhiwani, Haryana, where his parents were waiting to welcome him.The Dubai episode, he says, is now behind him. What remains is the lesson from it - and a much bigger target."Paris was very difficult for me to miss, but that experience made me stronger instead of breaking me. LA 2028 is obviously a very big goal for me," Kalkal said.And he is clear about what he wants from that opportunity. "Olympics mein jaana hai toh sirf participate karne ke liye nahi jaana, bhaisaab. Gold ke liye jaana hai [“If you’re going to the Olympics, don’t go just to participate, brother. Go there to win gold]."India had not won a wrestling gold at the Asian Games since 2018. Kalkal's victory ended that wait and added another major title to a career that already includes an U23 World Championship crown, Asian Championships success and a Zagreb Open triumph."India has won a wrestling gold at the Asian Games after eight years, so being a part of it is very special for me. This medal reminds me that if you keep working hard, your time will come," he said.The road to the Asian Games gold was not easy for Kalkal. He had a challenging draw, but handled each bout with confidence.After a comfortable opening victory, he made a statement in the quarterfinals by throwing Iran's Abbas Ebrahimzadehsavadkouhi from a standing position within the opening 20 seconds.The semifinal brought an even bigger test, but Kalkal overcame Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka to reach the gold medal bout.Then came the final against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev, and it looked like the toughest challenge of them all.Instead of allowing the deficit to affect him, Kalkal fought his way back into the contest. He produced eight points to turn a seven-point deficit into a 10-9 victory and seal the Asian Games title."The simple plan was to wrestle my own way and not be impressed by my opponent's name. Whether he is an Olympic champion, a world champion or anyone else, everyone starts from zero on the mat. I just trusted my preparation and my strength. I knew that if I executed my best, I could beat anyone. Instead of thinking too much during the match, I just had to fight for every single point," he said.Kalkal also dedicated the gold to the country and remembered his father, who stood by him throughout his journey."I dedicate this gold to the whole of India. Of course, my first call was to my father. He has supported me tremendously throughout this journey, and without his support, it would have been impossible for me to reach this point. His support will always remain with me," the Indian wrestler said.The final also reflected the mental change Kalkal says came from the disappointment of 2024."Fear may never completely go away, but now I know how to fight with fear. When you go through tough situations in life, small things stop bothering you. What happened in Dubai, missing the Olympic qualifiers - every experience taught me something," the Indian wrestler said."Now I don't run away from pressure. I enjoy pressure because those are the moments when you realise how strong you actually are," Kalkal said.The Asian Games gold now joins an already impressive list of achievements for Kalkal, but he is not dwelling on the medals he has already won. The next target is Los Angeles. And this time, he wants to get there on his own terms."Gold ke liye jaana hai."
Article Summary: Two years ago, Sujeet Kalkal was stranded at Dubai International Airport. He was on his way to Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, for the Asian Olympic Qualifying Tournament. Two years later, the disappointment of Dubai has been replaced by an Asian Games gold. He fought back from 2-9 down against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev.

Article Title: Other side of India's Asian Games success: 201 athletes won just 6 bronze, 137 returned empty-handed
Article Text:
AP Photo

The spending breakdown

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India’s 85-medal haul at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games was its secondbest finish, but the headline numbers don’t reveal everything.A sport-by-sport audit by TOI shows that 137 Indian athletes across 16 disciplines returned empty-handed, exposing persistent gaps in the country’s medal ambitions.India’s pruned-down 495-member contingent competed across 36 sport disciplines and finished fourth with 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals.Yet 137 athletes across 16 disciplines won nothing.Another 64 athletes across six sports managed six bronze — one each in kurash, mixed martial arts, rowing, sepaktakraw, soft tennis and wushu. The zero-medal list included canoeing (19 athletes), cycling (14), equestrian (7), esports (15), fencing (20), gymnastics (1), judo (3), karate (2), rugby sevens (13), sport climbing (2), surfing (4), swimming (12), taekwondo (3), tennis (7), teqball (3) and volleyball (12). The six-bronze group comprised kurash (6 athletes), MMA (2), rowing (22), sepaktakraw (21), soft tennis (6) and wushu (7).In all, 201 athletes accounted for just six bronze medals across the 22 disciplines mentioned above. In other prominent sports with sizable athlete numbers, table tennis sent 10 athletes and returned with one bronze and badminton’s 20-member contingent managed one bronze in the men’s team event.Together, the two sent 37 athletes and produced only two bronze.India contested in 259 medal events in AichiNagoya and won medals in just 20, a 7.7% eventpodium conversion rate. Of 356 medals available in which India featured, the nation collected 85, a conversion rate of only 23.9%.The govt spent Rs 259.69 crore on 19 sports as part of the overall total expenditure during the current Asian Games cycle (Nov 2023-Aug 2026), led by badminton (Rs 49.26 cr), cycling track (Rs 35.9 cr), fencing (Rs 28.2 cr), table tennis (Rs 25.3 cr), tennis (Rs 22.4 cr) and canoe/kayak (Rs 20.1 cr). Other allocations included rowing (Rs 13.8 cr,) swimming (Rs 10.8 cr), gymnastics (Rs 10.49 cr), judo (Rs 8.05 cr), wushu (Rs 7.8 cr), volleyball (Rs 6.5 cr), sepaktakraw (Rs 5.7 cr), equestrian (Rs 3.7 cr), rugby (Rs 3.63 cr), surfing (Rs 2.9 cr), karate (Rs 1.99 cr), soft tennis (Rs 1.6 cr) and kurash (Rs 1.6 cr).On three sports – MMA, eSports and sport climbing, the govt spent no money. As per the govt’s own estimates, it spent approximately Rs 703 cr across 30 disciplines during the Nov 2023-Aug 2026 preparation cycle. The Rs 703 cr included about Rs 118 cr for domestic training and national coaching camps, Rs 40 cr for overseas training, Rs 252 cr for international competition exposure, Rs 89 cr for equipment, Rs 86 cr for foreign coaches/support staff and Rs 118 cr for other expenses, including Indian experts, championships, competitions in India, grassroots and coach development.Also, a total of 427 athletes who were part of the govt’s various programmes and schemes participated in the Games, including 77 athletes from Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS) Core group, 78 from TOPS Development 78, 48 from Target Asian Games Group (TAGG), 65 Khelo India Athlete (KIA), 25 from National Centre of Excellence (NCoE) and 134 from National Coaching Camps (NCCs).The Glasgow comparison is revealing, though not like-for-like. India had 122 athletes and para-athletes in 10 sports at the curtailed 2026 Commonwealth Games and won 39 medals — 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze — also finishing fourth. The Asian Games contingent was 4.06 times larger, but its 85-medal haul was only 2.18 times Glasgow’s. Medal efficiency was 17.2 per 100 athletes in Aichi-Nagoya against 32 in Glasgow.The message is that at this level, the medal base remains concentrated.For a country investing Rs 703 cr across a multi-year cycle, the next challenge is clear: turn wider participation, exposure and support into wider podium conversion.
Article Summary: India’s pruned-down 495-member contingent competed across 36 sport disciplines and finished fourth with 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals. Of 356 medals available in which India featured, the nation collected 85, a conversion rate of only 23.9%. The govt spent Rs 259.69 crore on 19 sports as part of the overall total expenditure during the current Asian Games cycle.

NEW DELHI: India's wrestlers arrived in Aichi-Nagoya carrying questions over injuries, form and confidence. They left with six medals — two gold, two silver and two bronze — and a much bigger target already occupying their minds: the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.Aman Sehrawat and Sujeet Kalkal struck gold, while Nitesh Siwach and Antim Panghal won silver and Deepak Punia and Sunil Kumar added bronze.The campaign was also marked by two major statements. Sehrawat defeated reigning world champion Han Chong Song in the men's 57kg freestyle final, while Kalkal beat Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka on his way to gold in the 65kg category.For the Indian wrestlers, however, Nagoya was less about looking back at what they had achieved and more about building towards what comes next.For Sehrawat, the gold was the culmination of one of the most difficult phases of his young career.The 23-year-old had won bronze at the Paris Olympics but subsequently struggled with motivation in 2025. A persistent stomach ailment also forced him to miss important competitions.In Nagoya, however, Sehrawat rediscovered his best. He defeated reigning world champion Han Chong Song 11-7 in the final, recovering after the North Korean had turned a 1-6 deficit into a 7-6 lead.It was Sehrawat's first Asian Games gold after his bronze at Hangzhou."Ups and downs, injuries keep happening like this. The future goal is the Olympics," Sehrawat said after returning to India.He said the next goal was to replicate the achievement on the biggest stage."We won gold for the country. The plan for the future is exactly the same — we will win gold for the country and prepare accordingly. I thank all the countrymen; it was their prayers that worked in the matches," he added.Then came the statement that perhaps best captured the mood of India's wrestling contingent."...now we will do better in the future. The whole nation is giving us love. Now our national anthem will be played at the LA Olympics."If Sehrawat's gold was a comeback story, Kalkal's was a lesson in refusing to surrender.The world No. 2 entered the Asian Games unbeaten this season and lived up to his billing in the men's 65kg freestyle category.Before the final, Kalkal defeated Japan's Olympic champion Kiyooka and Iran's Abbas Ebrahimzadehsavadkouhi. Against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev in the final, he appeared to be heading towards defeat after falling 2-9 behind.Instead, he produced a stunning late comeback to win 10-9.The victory restored India's hold on the 65kg Asian Games title, a category in which Yogeshwar Dutt and Bajrang Punia had previously won gold."Whatever struggle I did has paid off. The final match was tough, but I was only thinking of winning that time," Kalkal said.His sights are already firmly fixed on Los Angeles."Now we will practice more, and if all goes well, we will win gold at the Olympics too. For the Olympics, the practice has already begun," Kalkal added.Nitesh Siwach's silver carried perhaps the most remarkable backstory of India's six medallists.A serious knee injury as a teenager kept him away from wrestling for more than 18 months. During that period, he helped his family with its dairy business and sold milk in Panipat.His comeback culminated in an historic Asian Games final appearance in the men's 97kg Greco-Roman category — India's first in the weight class in 64 years.Siwach eventually lost 0-4 to Japan's Yuri Nakazato but returned home with a silver medal and a clear Olympic target."I feel great. This is the first time I am getting such respect and honour. I am experiencing such a great welcome for the first time, and I am very happy," he said. "I had aimed for gold. I didn't win gold, but I did secure the silver medal and I am very happy about that. Since this was my first Asian Games, I am delighted with the silver."Siwach also believes India's Greco-Roman wrestlers can make their presence felt in Los Angeles."People used to say we wouldn't win medals in Greco-Roman, but we will continue to excel. We will bring home medals from the Los Angeles Olympics," he said.His personal target is even clearer."I made some mistakes, which is why I had to settle for silver. My goal going forward is to win gold at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, and I will work extremely hard for it," he added.He has already begun that preparation."My preparation for the Olympics has already begun, starting from the very day I won the medal. I have to bring a gold in the Olympics," Siwach said.Deepak Punia's bronze was another product of perseverance.The 2019 World Championships silver medallist had competed at 86kg and 92kg before moving to 97kg this year following a muscle injury.Despite the challenges of changing weight categories, Punia earned selection for the Asian Games and defeated Mongolia's Gankhuyag Ganbaatar 2-1 in the bronze-medal bout."Winning a medal was quite challenging for me because I used to compete in the 86kg category, but this time I participated in the 97kg category. There were many challenges, and my hope and goal was to win the gold medal. However, I had to settle for the bronze," Punia said.Experience helped him deal with the pressure."I have been playing for a long time, so there is pressure; there is pressure on every athlete. But I understood how I had to handle the pressure. In my mind, it was just that I had to give my best. It was not like I had to take over-pressure. I just had to give my 100 per cent and that's what I did," he said.Antim Panghal also upgraded her medal from bronze at Hangzhou to silver in the women's 53kg category.She lost 1-9 to Japan's Moe Kiyooka in the final after coaches had worked on keeping her calm and confident before the competition."It is my second time winning a medal. But I had thought that I had to come first, but I could not come first. In the future, I will try to do better than this," Panghal said.Sunil Kumar, meanwhile, returned to the podium after knee surgery to win bronze in the men's 87kg Greco-Roman category. He defeated the Philippines' Callum Johnston Roberts 9-0 by technical superiority, becoming the first Indian Greco-Roman wrestler to win two Asian Games medals after his bronze at Hangzhou."I am very happy and want to thank all my fellow countrymen. May your blessings and support continue to be with me," Kumar said.The six medals tell only part of India’s wrestling story in Nagoya.Sehrawat battled through a difficult phase to defeat a reigning world champion. Kalkal stunned an Olympic champion before producing a remarkable comeback for gold. Siwach overcame a serious teenage injury and years of struggle to reach a historic Greco-Roman final. Punia changed weight categories and still made the podium, while Panghal improved her medal colour and Kumar returned from knee surgery to make history.But beyond the six medals was a bigger message — India’s wrestlers are already looking towards Los Angeles.Their words after returning home reflected an ambition that goes far beyond Nagoya: to turn this success into Olympic gold in 2028.
Article Summary: Aman Sehrawat and Sujeet Kalkal struck gold, while Nitesh Siwach and Antim Panghal won silver. Deepak Punia and Sunil Kumar added bronze. India's wrestlers arrived in Aichi-Nagoya carrying questions over injuries, form and confidence. They left with six medals — two gold, two silver and two bronze.

Article Title: From ending South Korea’s reign to booking 2028 LA Olympics quotas: Indian archers return from Asian Games with bigger target
Article Text:
Gold medallist India's Kumkum Anil Mohod, Ankita Bhakat and Kirti celebrate on the podium during the victory ceremony. (Reuters Photo)

‘We proved exactly what they’re made of’

Gold medallists India's Chikitha Taniparthi and Sahil Rajesh Jadhav celebrate after winning the Compound Mixed Team Final. (Reuters Photo)

India's Kumkum Anil Mohod in action. (Reuters Photo)

‘We thought that we would do it, and we did’

India's Kumkum Anil Mohod, Ankita Bhakat and Kirti celebrate after winning the gold medal. (Reuters Photo)

Bigger target: LA 2028

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India's archers returned home from the Asian Games with more than a record medal haul to celebrate. They came back with history rewritten, Olympic qualification secured and the belief that the gap with the world's best is narrowing rapidly.The Indian contingent collected five gold, two silver and two bronze medals in Aichi-Nagoya, with both the compound and recurve squads producing landmark performances. The compound mixed team of Sahil Jadhav and Chikitha Taniparthu secured an Olympic quota place, while the recurve women's team ended South Korea's long-standing dominance by beating the 10-time Olympic champions 5-3 in the final.For a group that had faced questions before the Games, the response was emphatic. India's compound coach Dave Cousins believes the performance should put those doubts to rest.Cousins said the coaching group had deliberately avoided making medal predictions before the Games, instead focusing on preparation and execution.“So early on, they wanted us to make predictions on how many medals we could get. The only thing we were willing to commit to is that our athletes would go prepared and that they would execute the process as best they could,” Cousins said.The results, he argued, were a reflection of a stronger support system around the archers.“When the training is right, the preparation is right and the ecosystem is right, these are the results you get. So we're very happy with that. We're exceptionally happy to clinch the first ever compound archery spot for the Olympic Games. That's a huge thing for us right now,” he added.The success was particularly significant because much of the compound squad was relatively inexperienced on the biggest international stage.“You in the media and the global archery community really had a lot of questions about our younger archers, the new squad. Well, I think we proved exactly what they're made of,” Cousins said.Jadhav and Taniparthu were at the heart of that response. Their mixed-team gold not only delivered another Asian Games title but also secured India's Olympic quota place.Jadhav said the final against Chinese Taipei was less about pressure and more about sticking to a plan repeatedly rehearsed in training.“It feels fantastic, and seeing this grand welcome gives us even more joy. There wasn't pressure as such because we had practised specifically for these situations,” Jadhav said. “It was all about execution, and we delivered. Now I feel all the hard work I've put in so far has truly paid off.”Taniparthu said the victory had given the young group another reason to work harder.“This feels so good and happy, and by this we will get motivated that we have to win more, do more hard work, then every time we will also get this,” she said.The compound women's team also underlined India's growing strength by equalling the world record score during its 238-234 victory over China. Taniparthu won that gold alongside veteran Jyothi Surekha Vennam and Prithika Pradeep.Sahil was also part of the men's gold-medal-winning team, while Ganesh Mani Ratnam Thirumuru won men's team gold and individual bronze. Kushal Dalal was another member of the men's gold-winning side.The recurve contingent produced its own piece of history.Kumkum Mohod emerged as one of India's biggest individual stars, winning women's individual gold and helping the country secure women's team gold and mixed team silver. Her individual triumph also secured an Olympic quota for India.The 17-year-old said the result was the product of collective preparation rather than an individual effort.“What we thought would happen, happened. It was the team's hard work, all the team's motivation, and the support of the Archery Association of India and SAI. That's why everything happened,” she said.In the individual final against South Korea's Oh Yejin, Kumkum consciously shut out the opponent and concentrated on her own shooting.“In the final match, I completely enjoyed my shooting. I held on to my feeling, just shot my arrows and didn't look at who was ahead,” she said.Her advice after the breakthrough was equally simple.“Just stay disciplined and do your best at your work. Don't get carried away. Just keep doing your work properly,” she added.But it was the women's team victory over 10-time Olympic champions South Korea that arguably carried the biggest historical significance. Kirti Sharma was part of the side that defeated the Koreans 5-3, ending their dominance in the event.“India's first gold in this event. We beat Korea to win gold, so this created history for us. I feel very good that I was part of the team that created that history,” Sharma said.The magnitude of the challenge was not lost on the Indian team.“There was pressure because that team always took gold, so there was pressure on us, but we thought that we would do it, and we did,” Sharma said.The men's recurve squad also contributed to India's medal haul, with Dhiraj Bommadevara winning silver in the mixed team event with Kumkum and another silver in the men's team event. Neeraj Chauhan claimed individual bronze and men's team silver, while Yashdeep Bhoge was part of the silver-winning men's team.Bommadevara believes the support structure around Indian archery has changed dramatically.“Earlier, there was hardly any support, and I relied closely on my family and friends. But if it weren't for this government, I wouldn't be standing here today. Our Prime Minister, our Sports Minister and our administrative setup have been so supportive,” he said.The pressure of an Asian Games, he added, was easier to manage because of the team's environment.“Pressure is there for everyone, but we were fortunate to have a team where we could stay cool and calm,” he said.And the next targets are already visible.“Next year, we have the World Championships, where Olympic quotas are there, and after that the LA Olympics,” he said.For Chauhan, the Asian Games was his first experience of the multi-sport event, and the medal made the occasion even more meaningful.“Overall, the experience of the Asian Games was very good. It was my first Asian Games. I went with the hope that I had to bring a medal for India, and bringing this medal has made me and my family very proud,” he said.Bhoge, making his debut, highlighted the collective spirit that helped India navigate the crucial moments.“Obviously it was my debut, so there were crunch moments, but everyone kept their morale up. The team stayed together. Because the whole team stayed together, we were able to play well and maintain ourselves,” he said.The Asian Games medals have therefore brought celebration, but also a bigger expectation. With Olympic quotas secured, South Korea's recurve dominance finally broken and a new generation of compound archers announcing themselves, India's archery programme now has a new benchmark.The Aichi-Nagoya triumph was historic. The next target is bigger — Los Angeles 2028.
Article Summary: India's archers return home from the Asian Games with more than a record medal haul to celebrate. The Indian contingent collected five gold, two silver and two bronze medals in Aichi-Nagoya. The compound mixed team of Sahil Jadhav and Chikitha Taniparthu secured an Olympic quota place.

Vaibhav becomes India’s youngest medallist

Mairaj makes history at 50

The Asian Games 2026 took place in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, from September 19 to October 4, with athletes from 46 nations competing across various sports. India finished fourth in the medal table with 85 medals, including 21 golds, 27 silvers and 37 bronzes.India enjoyed several memorable performances, with the men’s and women’s teams winning gold medals in cricket, kabaddi and hockey. It was also the first time both Indian hockey teams won gold at the same Asian Games Among the standout individual performers was 17-year-old archer Kumkum Mohod, who became the first Indian woman to win individual recurve gold.She finished the Games with two golds and a silver. The teenage batting sensation was part of the Indian men’s cricket team that defeated Pakistan by 19 runs in the final to win gold.Sooryavanshi made an aggressive start, hitting two consecutive sixes, before Saim Ayub dismissed him for 15 off nine balls. Despite his early exit, India went on to win the final and secure a memorable gold medal.Two-time Olympian Mairaj Ahmad Khan became India’s oldest medallist at the 2026 Asian Games at the age of 50. He won bronze as part of the men’s skeet shooting team alongside Anantjeet Singh Naruka and Bhavtegh Singh Gill.Khan has competed internationally for more than 20 years and is a three-time ISSF World Cup gold medallist. However, the bronze in Aichi-Nagoya was his first Asian Games medal.Overall, Japan’s 11-year-old eSports player Yuki Kurihara became the youngest gold medallist in Asian Games history after winning the Puyo Puyo Champions title. Article Title: 'It's like water to a thirsty person': Asian Games gold reignites women's hockey at grassroots
Article Text:
Image credit: Hockey India

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

KOLKATA: The Indian women’s hockey team’s Asian Games gold medal after a 44-year wait has done more than secure direct qualification for the Olympics.According to coaches who have nurtured generations of players across the country, the triumph has rekindled belief at the grassroots, and is destined to inspire a new generation of girls to take up the sport while validating decades of hard work in academies and training centres, far from the spotlight.Former India captain Pritam Siwach, who has been working as a coach for more than 25 years in Sonipat, Haryana, believes the impact of the victory extends well beyond the podium.“This victory has given women’s hockey a new lease of life. It is like giving water to a thirsty person. Winning gold after 44 years has ended a long drought and brought renewed energy to the sport,” she said, adding that the success has given women’s hockey the recognition it deserves after years of operating in the shadow of the men’s game.For coaches working at the grassroots level, the medal has become a powerful tool. Dasrath Mahato, the 69-year-old from Khunti in Jharkhand who discovered and mentored Nikki Pradhan, said every major success creates a ripple effect among young athletes.“When children see players returning home with medals, they start to believe they can do the same. It inspires them to work harder and pursue hockey seriously,” Mahato said.The success has also been celebrated by coaches who have worked in some of the country’s leading hockey centres. Madhya Pradesh Hockey Academy coach Vandana says achievements at the elite level invariably strengthen the grassroots ecosystem.“When a sport performs well at the top level, it benefits the grassroots. We are already seeing more academies and leagues being established for women, and success like this will only accelerate that growth,” said Vandana, who trained the likes of Sushila Chanu and Bichu Devi Kharibam.Former India goalkeeper and coach Edgar Mascarenhas, who worked extensively in Odisha, described the achievement as one of the biggest milestones in the history of Indian women’s hockey.“I watched every match and what impressed me most was their fighting spirit. Even in difficult situations, they never gave up,” said Mascarenhas.The direct Olympic qualification has also been highlighted as one of the competition’s biggest outcomes. Coaches unanimously agreed that avoiding the pressure of an additional qualification campaign allows the team to focus entirely on preparation for the Games.“This may actually be even more important than the gold medal itself,” said Siwach. “Now the players know they are going to the Olympics and can devote all their energy towards preparing for that challenge.”The impact has been felt in regions that have emerged as strong contributors to Indian women’s hockey. In Mizoram, where coach Miss Btei helped nurture internationals Lalremsiami and Lalthantluangi, interest in the sport continues to grow among young children.“The success of players from our state will encourage more youngsters to take up hockey. Children see what Lalremsiami has achieved and begin to believe they can follow the same path,” she said.According to Btei, players as young as nine or ten years old, are now entering the development pathway with the latest generation already benefiting from the visibility created by the national team’s success.For former India international and coach Ajit Lakra, the gold medal represents proof that India’s grassroots structures are delivering results.“These players came through the grassroots system and delivered a gold-medal performance that resonated across Asia. It shows young athletes that there is a pathway from the grassroots level to the international stage,” said Lakra, who coached Rutuja Dadaso Pisal.While they welcomed the growing number of opportunities for women, the coaches stressed the importance of greater investment in infrastructure, academies and player development programmes to sustain the momentum.Yet the overriding sentiment remains one of optimism. Whether in hockey strongholds like Jharkhand and Odisha, established academies in Madhya Pradesh or emerging centres like Mizoram, coaches see the medal as a catalyst for growth.
Article Summary: The Indian women's hockey team's Asian Games gold medal after a 44-year wait has done more than secure direct qualification for the Olympics. The triumph has rekindled belief at the grassroots, and is destined to inspire a new generation of girls to take up the sport.

Article Title: UCL Round-up: Barcelona, Arsenal pick up convincing wins; Inter Milan, Manchester United suffer defeats
Article Text:
Barcelona's Joao Cancelo, right, celebrates with teammates after scoring his side's first goal during the Champions League opening phase soccer match between Galatasaray and Barcelona in Istanbul, Turkey, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. (AP Photo/Khalil Hamra)

Barcelona bounce back, Bayern suffer late heartbreak

Arsenal shine as Manchester United struggle

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Barcelona and Arsenal secured convincing wins in the Champions League on Tuesday, while Bayern Munich suffered a late setback against Viking in Norway.Meanwhile, Manchester United’s poor form continued with a 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid, increasing pressure on coach Michael Carrick.Barcelona came from behind to beat Galatasaray 4-1 in Istanbul, extending its winning streak to 10 games in all competitions.Arsenal also impressed with a 3-0 victory over Lille, while Inter Milan suffered a surprising 4-3 home defeat to Club Brugge.Barcelona faced an early challenge when Aleksey Batrakov put Galatasaray ahead. However, Joao Cancelo equalized just before halftime, and Barcelona took control in the second half. Goals from Fermin Lopez, Anthony Gordon and Karim Adeyemi sealed the win.“In the second half, we dominated the game,” Barcelona coach Hansi Flick said. “We have to play like this, control the game, move the ball. This is our quality. This is our strength, and we have to show our level.”Bayern Munich, meanwhile, were left frustrated after throwing away a lead against Viking. Trailing 2-0 at halftime, Bayern fought back through two Harry Kane goals before Luis Diaz made it 3-2.However, Michael Olise was sent off after receiving two yellow cards, and Herman Haugen scored a 90th-minute equalizer to secure a 3-3 draw.“We were dominant, but at the moment it feels like every chance for the opposition leads to a goal," Bayern coach Vincent Kompany said.Arsenal defeated Lille 3-0, with Jurrien Timber opening the scoring before substitute Bukayo Saka made an immediate impact. Saka set up a goal for Eberechi Eze and scored himself shortly after coming on.Manchester United’s struggles continued as Atletico Madrid won 2-0 through goals from Pablo Barrios and Ademola Lookman. United defender Lisandro Martinez criticized the club’s recruitment and called for more support from the management.“I expect more from our technical director. I would have to be honest, as the players, we have to do more, but it’s just important when you make a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night.”Elsewhere, Nicolo Tresoldi scored a hat trick as Club Brugge stunned Inter Milan 4-3. Villarreal beat Napoli 3-1, while Azerbaijani club Sabah earned its first league-phase win with a 2-0 victory over Slavia Prague.Sporting Lisbon also won 2-0 against Lens, and Leipzig defeated PSV Eindhoven 1-0.
Article Summary: Barcelona comes from behind to beat Galatasaray 4-1 in Istanbul. Arsenal also impressed with a 3-0 victory over Lille, while Inter Milan suffered a surprising 4-3 home defeat to Club Brugge. Manchester United’s poor form continued with a 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid, increasing pressure on coach Michael Carrick.

Article Title: Lisandro Martinez blasts Manchester United hierarchy in fiery rant; Wayne Rooney brands comments ‘disrespectful’ after UCL loss to Atletico Madrid
Article Text:
Lisandro Martinez and Wayne Rooney

Wayne Rooney questions Martinez’s motives

Rooney draws on his own experience

Ashley Young backs Rooney’s assessment

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez has sparked controversy after openly criticising the club’s hierarchy following a 2-0 Champions League defeat to Atletico Madrid, with former United captain Wayne Rooney accusing the Argentine of being disrespectful to his teammates.The defender’s post-match interview raised questions about United’s summer recruitment strategy and the club’s readiness to compete at the highest level. Martinez expressed frustration with the lack of further investment in the squad, suggesting that the club’s decision-makers should have done more after the team secured its return to the Champions League.Speaking to Amazon Prime, Martinez said: “I have to control myself a lot. But sometimes it’s a reflection in the mirror of how is our club at the moment,” Martinez told Amazon Prime. “We did a fantastic season last season. And now we expect more from the top, from up, to bring more players to compete because many teams bring many players as well, and today also Atletico they have an amazing team and they deserved to win today.“I expect more from our technical director. I would have to be honest, as the players, we have to do more, but it’s just important when you make a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night.”United, under director of football Jason Wilcox, reportedly invested around $213 million during the summer transfer window, bringing in players including Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos. Despite that spending, the club has endured a disappointing start to the campaign.The defeat in Madrid extended United’s winless streak across all competitions to five matches. The team has managed just one Premier League victory and currently sits 13th in the standings.Martinez also reflected on the contrast between last season’s progress and the team’s current struggles, expressing disappointment with the performance in Spain.“Last season we did everything; we created the base to be an amazing team,” Martinez said. “It's annoying, disappointing to come here and I'm not seeing my team trying to get an amazing result here, it's disappointing.”Atletico made an immediate impact, with Pablo Barrios scoring in the opening minute before Ademola Lookman added a second-half goal to secure the victory. The result has increased scrutiny on United head coach Michael Carrick as the club attempts to recover from its difficult start.However, Martinez suggested that the focus on managerial changes overlooks other issues within the organisation.“You start changing, changing, changing manager. But what about other areas?” Martinez said. “I can’t say more.”Rooney strongly disagreed with Martinez’s decision to air his frustrations publicly, arguing that concerns about recruitment and squad quality should be discussed internally rather than through the media.Speaking on Amazon Prime after the match, the former United striker said: "I actually disagree as I thought it was a good performance."It's a difficult one because I always used to feel like I was outspoken as a player, and you want to have your opinion, but I think he's maybe gone too far; that should be down to the manager, and that should stay internal because the fans want to hear the players speak and they want to see them care."He clearly cares and wants the club to invest more money and more players, and if they do that, I think he'll be one of the players out the door if I'm being honest with his performances."His performances haven't been good enough but I think in some ways he is right, in terms of the club need to invest more at the top end of the pitch and in defence as well."I think it looks like that was a bit of an agenda from him because that doesn't mirror the performance. I thought the performance was better."Although Rooney acknowledged that United need improvements in key areas, he questioned why Martinez chose that particular moment to make his concerns public."I think Martinez was very premeditated. Why is he doing the interview after this game? Has he put himself forward, I very rarely hear him speak."It looked a bit premeditated and something he spoke about with his team to get out there. It's sad because when you need everyone to stick together as players, you can't be told what's going on above you."So you need them players, the manager, the coaching staff to stick together when you're having a difficult time; otherwise, something like that will rip a dressing room apart."I think it's a bit disrespectful to his team-mates as well because he's disrespecting his team-mates, he's saying they're not good enough. So he's saying his team-mates aren't good enough, so it's disrespectful."Rooney also suggested that captain Bruno Fernandes would be better placed to raise concerns on behalf of the squad, while insisting that any issues should be addressed privately."I think Bruno is probably the only one who has any right coming out and saying something like that if I'm being honest as captain. And even then, it should be behind closed doors if there are issues, which does happen."Players have conversations with the manager, the manager then has a conversation with the board, but that interview there, it's not going to help the situation the club is in at the minute."Now all that's going to bring is more noise around it, the players are unhappy, they're unsettled, they don't trust in their own team-mates, that's not going to help at all."Rooney went further when discussing whether Martinez was attempting to reflect the frustrations of Manchester United supporters. While expressing appreciation for the defender’s ability, he pointed to his injury record and questioned whether he had done enough to speak on behalf of the squad."I don't think he's really connected with the fans since he's been here, to be honest, because he's been injured a lot."I actually like him, I think he's a good player, but he's been injured, so for the money the Man United pay for him, he hasn't given the service back really."From that point of view, that's not me being disrespectful, I just think he's had a lot of injuries and hasn't played that much."So I think he's trying to speak on behalf of the players if you like, but I think he's done it in the wrong way, as I said before, I think that should be from the captain if that's the case."For me, it's disrespectful to his teammates. I had a similar situation when I went in and asked Alex Ferguson about what players we were bringing in, and I apologised two days later."So I can speak from experience of what he's just done, I think it is very disrespectful, there's a lot of young players in that dressing room as well that need some guidance from experienced players."Drawing on his own playing career, Rooney argued that experienced footballers have a responsibility to guide younger teammates, particularly during difficult periods. He also indicated that the club’s board may need to respond to Martinez’s remarks."The board have to look at that, and they probably have to take some action on that, because that's just disrespecting the whole football club."Yes, there's issues, everyone wants more players and better players, but this is the players you've got. As a player, you've got to get on with it."You've got to go and show why you're a World Cup winner, as I said before. So, I think the board have to either come out and speak on it, or maybe he's done that to flush them out and get them to speak to the fans, but I just think it's the wrong time, and it's not going to help anyone."Former Manchester United player Ashley Young also questioned Martinez’s timing, agreeing that the club’s recruitment process needs improvement but stressing that players must take responsibility for their performances.Young acknowledged that United could have strengthened other areas of the squad during the summer, particularly in attack and defence. However, he argued that rebuilding the team cannot happen all at once."Of course, there is a lot of it that the players are talking about it. We spoke before the game about how the club needed to invest more, but when they've invested in the midfield but what does he want?"Go and buy a whole new team? They're not going to do that. They need to start in different positions. They could've bought up front or in defence but they didn't. He's just come off the pitch, emotions are running high, we know that."But we know the recruitment has to work, it has to be better but they've got to take time and do it. The players have got to take it upon themselves, 'we're the players that are in this team, we're the players that are in this squad and go out on the pitch.'"They are the ones who have to go and produce and show what they're about. There's not going to be any change now until January."With the January transfer window still some way off, United face mounting pressure to improve results with their existing squad.Martinez’s criticism has highlighted concerns about recruitment and the club’s direction, but Rooney and Young believe that publicly airing such frustrations risks creating further divisions inside the dressing room at a time when unity is crucial.
Article Summary: Lisandro Martinez criticises Manchester United hierarchy after 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid. Former United captain Wayne Rooney accuses Martinez of being disrespectful to his team-mates. United have endured a disappointing start to the season, with just one Premier League win.

Article Title: Atletico Madrid captain Koke loses mother just hours before Manchester United clash in heartbreaking news for club
Article Text:
Atletico Madrid captain Koke mourns his mother’s passing as Manchester United offer condolences ahead of their Champions League clash.

Atletico confirm Koke’s mother has died

Manchester United offer condolences ahead of kick-off
